report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: use thin, crystalline, optically transparent muscovite mica as a polymer-free van der Waals transfer medium whose adhesion to 2D materials is tuned by temperature, enabling deterministic pick-up, stacking, and release without organic polymer contact. Atomic-force-microscopy-grade muscovite crystals are mechanically exfoliated with adhesive tape to produce few-hundred-nanometer-thick mica layers. For membrane stamps, a mica sheet is suspended over a 5–6 mm punched hole in Nitto ELP BT-50E-FR tape or several layers of Scotch Magic tape, transferred onto a rectangular PDMS block on a microscope glass slide, and tensioned by fixing the tape to the glass-slide sides. For cantilever stamps, a triangular mica sheet is cleaved from the tape edge, mounted on a metal support angled about 15 degrees on a microscope glass slide, and used as a freestanding transparent cantilever. Source mica and prepared stamps are stored under inert gas or in a dry vacuum desiccator; transfers are performed in argon glove-box or air conditions with ambient relative humidity kept below about 50% to limit water adsorption. For hBN/graphene/hBN assembly, a Si/SiO2 substrate containing an hBN flake is preheated to 50–90 °C, the mica stamp is brought into contact under an optical microscope by z-axis motion, the contact front is moved by z approach or by changing substrate temperature within ±10 °C, and full contact is made with the target flake before retraction. Subsequent 2D layers such as graphene are picked up using the already collected top hBN. For release, a target substrate carrying a bottom hBN flake is heated to 120–180 °C; the stack is brought into contact with the bottom hBN and the contact front is swept by temperature variation while leaving part of the bottom hBN uncovered by mica to test selective release of only the intended stack. The spatial scope is optical-microscope-guided flake-scale transfer over tens of micrometers in the active heterostructure region, using the mica membrane or cantilever as the only solid transfer support in place of PC/PPC polymer.

result_rows.description: Whether the mica membrane or cantilever protocol produced the intended hBN/graphene/hBN van der Waals heterostructure without a polymer transfer layer contacting the stack.
Whether the temperature-controlled mica protocol enabled release of the intended stack onto bottom hBN while retaining unwanted picked-up flakes on the mica stamp.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: evaluate whether the polymer-free mica cantilever transfer leaves atomically flat, clean hBN-encapsulated graphene interfaces without solvent cleaning or annealing. A single-layer graphene flake is fully encapsulated between top and bottom hBN using mica-cantilever-assisted assembly and the standard bottom-hBN release mechanism. The released stack is characterized as-is by contact-mode atomic force microscopy over the working area of the heterostructure, with the roughness extracted from a defined interior analysis window inside a several-micrometer AFM scan, away from visible flake edges and macroscopic contamination pockets. The measurement targets surface height variations of the top hBN over the active graphene-containing region after polymer-free release.

result_rows.description: The root-mean-square topographic roughness of the mica-cantilever-assembled hBN-encapsulated single-layer graphene stack measured in the selected AFM analysis window.
The peak-to-peak topographic roughness of the mica-cantilever-assembled hBN-encapsulated single-layer graphene stack measured in the selected AFM analysis window.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: test a polymer-free bottom-up assembly route in which a mica cantilever is incorporated as the supporting substrate by flipping the assembly and mechanically breaking off the cantilever, avoiding reliance on an additional bottom hBN release flake. A single-layer graphene flake is encapsulated in hBN on a graphite gate electrode using a mica cantilever; the cantilever is then flipped, broken off, and retained below the heterostructure as a mica layer. The sample is examined as-is by contact-mode AFM on the active hBN/graphene/hBN/graphite region, with roughness calculated from an interior analysis box inside a several-micrometer scan, away from flake boundaries and visible defects. The measurement targets whether the mica-supported heterostructure has an atomically flat exposed top surface after the polymer-free break-off release.

result_rows.description: The root-mean-square topographic roughness of the mica-supported hBN-encapsulated single-layer graphene stack measured in the selected AFM analysis window.
The peak-to-peak topographic roughness of the mica-supported hBN-encapsulated single-layer graphene stack measured in the selected AFM analysis window.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: determine whether the mica membrane method can assemble a more complex multilayer van der Waals stack with clean interfaces and without post-transfer cleaning. A seven-layer heterostructure is assembled by mica-membrane-assisted transfer with the layer sequence hBN / twisted trilayer graphene / hBN / graphite / hBN; each graphene layer in the twisted trilayer graphene is intentionally misaligned by a high angle of about 20 degrees to decouple the graphene layers. The stack is released and characterized as-is without annealing, solvent immersion, or other cleaning. Contact-mode AFM is performed on the active multilayer region over an area exceeding 100 µm², and topographic roughness is extracted from an interior analysis window away from visible edges and bubbles. The measurement targets the surface flatness of the exposed top hBN above the multilayer graphene/graphite structure.

result_rows.description: The root-mean-square topographic roughness of the mica-membrane-assembled hBN/twisted-trilayer-graphene/hBN/graphite/hBN stack measured in the selected AFM analysis window.
The peak-to-peak topographic roughness of the mica-membrane-assembled hBN/twisted-trilayer-graphene/hBN/graphite/hBN stack measured in the selected AFM analysis window.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: assess whether mica-assisted assembly can produce a clean, marginally twisted hBN/hBN moiré ferroelectric superlattice over a large flake-scale area, using the atomically flat mica surface and low-temperature release to preserve the twist configuration. A cracked hBN flake is used so that one piece is picked up with a mica membrane and released back onto another part of the same hBN flake at 50 °C, targeting marginal angular alignment. The resulting hBN/hBN stack is characterized by AFM height imaging and Kelvin probe force microscopy under scanning-probe conditions. The KPFM scans target nanoscale electrostatic-potential modulation associated with triangular ferroelectric moiré domains over the top hBN flake, including a large-area scan of the whole flake-scale region and a higher-resolution scan near a localized submicron interfacial bubble to test continuity and local deformation of the domain pattern.

result_rows.description: Whether the marginally twisted hBN/hBN structure produced by mica-assisted assembly exhibited a ferroelectric moiré superlattice detectable by KPFM.
The approximate area of the top hBN flake over which the ferroelectric moiré domains extended in KPFM characterization.
The approximate fabrication yield for hBN-based moiré superlattice structures using the mica-assisted protocol, as reported for this structure class.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: compare the mica-assisted polymer-free route with a conventional polycarbonate-based assembly for marginally twisted hBN/hBN moiré ferroelectrics, focusing on whether surface residues obstruct scanning-probe detection of the interfacial moiré potential. A marginally twisted hBN/hBN structure is assembled using a standard PC-assisted method, most of the PC is dissolved in dichloromethane for several hours, and the exposed surface is examined by KPFM before and after local contact-mode AFM mechanical cleaning. The scan covers both polymer-residue-covered regions and an AFM-cleaned region on the hBN/hBN stack, using the same type of ferroelectric moiré electrostatic contrast targeted in the mica-assisted hBN/hBN measurement.

result_rows.description: Whether polymer residues on the PC-assembled hBN/hBN stack screened the KPFM-detectable moiré ferroelectric potential in residue-covered regions.
Whether local contact-mode AFM cleaning enabled KPFM detection of the hBN/hBN moiré ferroelectric potential in the cleaned region.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: test whether a pre-characterized marginally aligned single-layer graphene/hBN moiré heterostructure can be picked up by a mica membrane while preserving the moiré wavelength and therefore the twist angle. A single-layer graphene on hBN stack is first assembled on SiO2/Si by a PC-based method and characterized by peak-force microscopy in a clean area between PC-residue traces. The heterostructure is then picked up using a mica membrane at 50 °C and re-characterized with the same AFM cantilever while supported by mica. Peak-force microscopy line profiles are compared along defined line cuts in the pre-pickup and post-pickup scans over a nanoscale moiré region, targeting the periodic adhesion or indentation modulation of the SLG/hBN moiré lattice rather than macroscopic flake morphology.

result_rows.description: The SLG/hBN moiré wavelength measured by peak-force microscopy before mica pickup while the heterostructure was on SiO2/Si.
The SLG/hBN moiré wavelength measured by peak-force microscopy after pickup onto the mica membrane.
Whether comparison of the SLG/hBN moiré wavelength before and after mica pickup indicated preservation of the twist angle.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: use polymer-free mica-membrane assembly to expose clean conductive twisted bilayer graphene surfaces for high-resolution conductive AFM, while deterministically setting sub-degree twist angles to tune the moiré period. Marginal-angle twisted bilayer graphene devices are assembled on thick graphite flakes by the mica-membrane method with nominal twist angles of about 0.8°, 0.3°, and 0.15°. Conductive AFM is performed in ambient air at room temperature with relative humidity below 56% using a Bruker Dimension Icon AFM, Nanoscope VII controller, PFTUNA module, and Pt-coated Si CONTV-PT tip of approximate radius 25 nm and spring constant about 0.2 N/m. Scanning is in contact mode at 0.5–1 Hz. The 0.8° scan uses 1 mV sample bias, -0.1 V deflection setpoint, and 256 × 256 pixels; the 0.3° scans use 0.4 mV bias, 0.02 V setpoint, and 512 × 512 or 256 × 256 pixels; the 0.15° scans use 7 mV bias, 0.08 V or 0.05 V setpoint, and 512 × 512 or 256 × 256 pixels. Current maps are first-order flattened. The scans span nanoscale fields of view from tens to hundreds of nanometers and target local tip-sample current variation associated with AA/AB/BA domains and domain walls, with the broader uniformity context assessed across up to micrometer-scale exposed TBG surface.

result_rows.description: The moiré period measured by conductive AFM for the approximately 0.8° twisted bilayer graphene device.
Whether conductive AFM resolved AA, AB, and BA domain contrast and associated domain-wall structure in the lower-angle twisted bilayer graphene devices.
The approximate maximum area over which the exposed twisted bilayer graphene moiré superlattice was reported to remain uniform and clean for cAFM/STM-scale studies.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: determine whether mica-assisted assembly yields graphene Hall-bar electronic quality comparable to state-of-the-art clean van der Waals devices. A large-area hBN/single-layer-graphene/hBN heterostructure is assembled on SiO2/Si using the mica-assisted method and patterned into a Hall bar in a bubble-free region with approximate dimensions 20 µm by 14 µm. Low-temperature multiterminal non-local bend-resistance measurements are performed at T = 1.7 K. Charge-carrier density n is swept over approximately -1.5 × 10^12 to +1.0 × 10^12 cm^-2 and perpendicular magnetic field B over approximately -0.3 to +0.3 T in the non-local geometry, with current and voltage probes arranged across the Hall-bar width. The measurement targets ballistic transport signatures, magnetic electron focusing, and mobility as functions of carrier density in the active encapsulated graphene channel.

result_rows.description: Whether the hBN-encapsulated single-layer graphene Hall bar exhibited negative non-local resistance at zero magnetic field in the bend-resistance geometry.
Whether the non-local magnetotransport exhibited magnetic electron focusing oscillations.
The electron mobility reached at high carrier density in the hBN-encapsulated single-layer graphene Hall bar.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: test the mica-assisted method on a complex, high-angle twisted trilayer graphene heterostructure where low disorder and ballisticity are probed by low-field Landau quantization. A seven-layer hBN/twisted-trilayer-graphene/hBN/graphite/hBN heterostructure assembled by the mica membrane method, with the three graphene layers intentionally misaligned by high angles of about 20°, is fabricated into a Hall bar on SiO2/Si. Low-temperature non-local bend-resistance is measured as a function of total carrier density n and perpendicular magnetic field B, with an applied displacement field condition D = -0.5 V/nm for the non-local map. A double-gate resistance map is also measured at fixed B = 50 mT while sweeping carrier density over approximately -0.2 × 10^12 to +0.2 × 10^12 cm^-2 and displacement field over approximately -0.2 to +0.2 V/nm. The measurement targets ballistic bend resistance and the onset and multiplicity of Landau quantization from the top, middle, and bottom graphene layers.

result_rows.description: Whether the high-angle twisted trilayer graphene Hall bar exhibited negative bend resistance at zero magnetic field.
The magnetic-field scale at which Landau quantization became detectable in the high-angle twisted trilayer graphene Hall bar.
The reported lower bound on the number of distinct Landau levels observed in the double-gate map at 50 mT.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: evaluate whether a heterostructure assembled on a mica cantilever and released by flipping and breaking off the cantilever can function as a high-quality gated graphene Hall-bar device with mica retained as part of the substrate stack. An hBN-encapsulated single-layer graphene heterostructure on a bottom graphite gate is assembled on a freestanding mica cantilever, then flipped and mechanically broken off so the mica remains below the stack. The device is patterned into a Hall bar; the bottom graphite is used as a bottom gate and Ti/Au is used as a top gate, with metal contacts routed over the several-hundred-nanometer-thick mica support. Longitudinal resistivity is measured versus gate voltage during ascending and descending gate sweeps at T = 300 K and again after cooling to T = 1.5 K. Mean free path is extracted at T = 1.5 K as a function of carrier density and compared with the Hall-bar width indicated by the device geometry. The measurement targets hysteresis, Dirac-peak asymmetry, and whether the electronic mean free path reaches the geometric limit.

result_rows.description: Whether the mica-supported hBN-encapsulated graphene Hall bar exhibited gate-sweep hysteresis at room temperature.
Whether the mica-supported graphene Hall bar exhibited a large asymmetry of the Dirac peak between opposite gate-sweep directions.
Whether the extracted low-temperature electron mean free path was limited by the Hall-bar width.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: use solvent-free mica-assisted transfer to fabricate suspended 2D heterostructure membranes suitable for nanomechanics, avoiding liquid processing that can damage suspended devices. A single-layer graphene/hBN heterostructure is assembled with the same mica-assisted transfer conditions used for supported stacks and suspended over a circular hole etched in a bottom hBN flake on SiO2, forming a membrane with diameter d = 3 µm. The membrane surface is inspected by peak-force microscopy over the suspended region to target surface continuity and cleanliness. Static force-deflection AFM is then performed at the center of the suspended membrane; force is swept up to approximately 800 nN while indentation is recorded up to approximately 50 nm. The force-deflection curve is fit to the standard continuum-mechanics model for a circular membrane, extracting Young's modulus E and pre-tension N0, where E is the in-plane elastic modulus of the suspended heterostructure membrane and N0 is the built-in membrane tension per unit length.

result_rows.description: Whether the mica-assisted procedure produced a suspended single-layer graphene/hBN heterostructure membrane over the etched hBN cavity.
The Young's modulus extracted from continuum-mechanics fitting of the static AFM force-deflection curve of the suspended SLG/hBN membrane.
The membrane pre-tension per unit length extracted from continuum-mechanics fitting of the static AFM force-deflection curve of the suspended SLG/hBN membrane.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: characterize the dynamic nanomechanical response of a solvent-free mica-transferred suspended single-layer graphene/hBN heterostructure membrane. The same circular d = 3 µm SLG/hBN membrane suspended over an hBN cavity is mounted inside an Attocube attoDRY800 optical cryostat on an xy positioning stage and cooled to T = 4 K under high vacuum. A power-modulated blue diode laser with wavelength 450 nm actuates membrane motion, and a HeNe red laser with wavelength 633 nm reads out displacement interferometrically; both laser spots are about 1 µm and incident laser powers are below 1 µW. The response amplitude is processed by a vector network analyzer while sweeping drive frequency over the fundamental-mode resonance region around 23.4–24.2 MHz. The resonance spectrum is fit to a linear damped harmonic-oscillator model to extract the resonance frequency f0 and mechanical quality factor Q.

result_rows.description: The fundamental mechanical resonance frequency extracted from the damped harmonic-oscillator fit of the suspended SLG/hBN membrane response.
The mechanical quality factor extracted from the damped harmonic-oscillator fit of the suspended SLG/hBN membrane response.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: extend mica-assisted solvent-free transfer to suspended moiré membranes, where substrate-free aligned graphene/hBN superlattices can be examined by scanning probe methods. An aligned single-layer graphene/hBN heterostructure, with the hBN component being 1–2 layers, is fabricated by mica-assisted transfer and suspended over a pre-etched circular cavity in hBN with diameter d = 0.5 µm. Peak-force microscopy adhesion mapping is performed over the full suspended membrane area with nanoscale lateral resolution to target the periodic adhesion modulation of the SLG/hBN moiré lattice across the free-standing region, including assessment of whether the periodic pattern extends to the membrane boundary rather than being limited to a supported substrate region.

result_rows.description: Whether the mica-assisted transfer produced a suspended aligned SLG/hBN moiré heterostructure membrane over the hBN cavity.
Whether the PFM adhesion map detected the SLG/hBN moiré pattern over the suspended membrane surface.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: test whether mica cantilevers can manipulate non-graphene van der Waals ferroelectrics without polymer residues, using folded 3R-MoS2 as a target structure relevant for mirror-twin-boundary ferroelectric interfaces. A large 3R-MoS2 flake is contacted by a mica cantilever; part of the flake is picked up, folded onto itself, and then delaminated and released by sliding the flake off the cantilever while moving parallel to the substrate surface. The resulting folded and unfolded 3R-MoS2 regions are characterized by AFM over interior areas of each region, away from the fold edge and macroscopic flake boundaries. The measurement targets the topographic roughness of the polymer-free folded interface and the adjacent original region.

result_rows.description: Whether the mica-cantilever folding and sliding release procedure produced a folded 3R-MoS2 structure.
The peak-to-peak topographic roughness of the folded 3R-MoS2 region measured by AFM.
The peak-to-peak topographic roughness of the adjacent unfolded 3R-MoS2 region measured by AFM.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: demonstrate that mica-assisted polymer-free transfer can produce open, uncapped monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenide heterostructures with clean surfaces suitable for optical measurements. A monolayer MoS2 flake is transferred onto an hBN substrate using the mica-assisted procedure; for materials other than hBN, the mica may be mildly treated by UV/O3 at 60 °C for 12 min to improve adhesion. The uncapped MoS2/hBN stack is characterized in ambient air at room temperature. AFM height mapping is used to assess the top surface over the monolayer flake region, and photoluminescence spectroscopy is collected over the visible spectral window corresponding to wavelengths 550–750 nm, targeting the MoS2 excitonic emission from the transferred monolayer.

result_rows.description: The root-mean-square surface roughness of the uncapped monolayer MoS2 on hBN measured by AFM.
The photoluminescence peak energy of the uncapped monolayer MoS2 on hBN measured in air at room temperature.
The full width at half maximum of the room-temperature photoluminescence peak of the uncapped monolayer MoS2 on hBN.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: assess the broader material compatibility of the mica-assisted polymer-free transfer method beyond graphene and hBN, including exposed conductive layers and air-sensitive magnetic crystals. The same mica-assisted pick-up, stacking, and release strategy is applied to fabricate open single-layer graphene on hBN, hBN-encapsulated few-layer CrBr3, and few-layer FePS3 on hBN. Transfers are performed under dry or inert conditions compatible with mica adhesion control; for top materials with weaker adhesion than hBN, mild UV/O3 treatment of mica at 60 °C for 12 min may be used. Optical microscopy is used over tens-of-micrometers flake-scale areas to assess whether the intended target flakes remain continuous and positioned on the hBN supports or encapsulated between hBN layers, with special attention to the uncapped or air-sensitive active material regions.

result_rows.description: Whether the mica-assisted method produced an uncapped single-layer graphene on hBN heterostructure.
Whether the mica-assisted method produced an hBN-encapsulated few-layer CrBr3 heterostructure.
Whether the mica-assisted method produced a few-layer FePS3 on hBN heterostructure.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: characterize environmental control of mica adhesion, which underlies the temperature-tunable polymer-free transfer mechanism. Adhesion forces between gold-plated mica cantilevers and representative surfaces including graphite, hBN, and SiO2 are measured by AFM force-deflection methods in ambient conditions while varying humidity and substrate temperature. High-humidity conditions are defined as relative humidity above about 60%, and low-humidity transfer-relevant conditions are compared while increasing the substrate temperature above room temperature up to the range in which the transfer protocol operates. The measurement targets the contact adhesion force between mica and the 2D-material or substrate surfaces, particularly the sensitivity of mica-hBN adhesion to adsorbed water and the reduction of adhesion at elevated temperature.

result_rows.description: The approximate multiplicative increase in mica-hBN adhesion force under high-humidity conditions relative to lower-humidity conditions.
The lower bound of the substrate-temperature range where the reduced adhesion force reaches a plateau under low-humidity conditions.
The upper bound of the substrate-temperature range where the reduced adhesion force reaches a plateau under low-humidity conditions.

per_file.paper_title: Dynamics of wavepackets and entanglement in many-body kicked rotors under quantum resonance

expected_output.experiment_description: Numerical Floquet simulation of the two-rotor kicked-rotor model used to illustrate the paper's symmetry-selection mechanism connecting wavepacket spreading and entanglement. The kicking potential is V(theta_1,theta_2)=k_1 cos(theta_1)+k_2 cos(theta_2)+xi cos(theta_1-theta_2), with k_1=0.1, k_2=0.2, and xi=1. Rotor 1 is set at the principal quantum resonance tau_1=4*pi and rotor 2 at the secondary quantum resonance tau_2=2*pi; hbar=T=1. The initial state is the product momentum eigenstate |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>. The bipartition for entanglement is rotor 1 versus rotor 2, and linear entropy is S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2). The simulation evaluates <p_1^2(t)> over kick steps shown on a logarithmic time axis up to t=1000, and <p_2^2(t)> and S_lin(t) over kick steps up to t=100. The central concept tested is that the partial π translation of the secondary-resonant rotor makes the rotor-1 effective potential mixed-symmetry, the rotor-2 effective potential antisymmetric, and the inter-rotor coupling antisymmetric, so the measured quantities target hybrid, anti-resonant, and entanglement-oscillatory responses respectively.

p1_variance_quadratic_coefficient_lambda.description: The coefficient of the quadratic component of the rotor-1 momentum variance.

p1_variance_odd_step_oscillation_magnitu.description: The magnitude of the odd-step oscillatory component in the rotor-1 momentum variance.

p1_wavepacket_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of the rotor-1 wavepacket variance.

p2_variance_odd_step_oscillation_magnitu.description: The odd-step oscillation magnitude of the rotor-2 momentum variance.

p2_wavepacket_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of the rotor-2 wavepacket variance.

odd_step_linear_entropy.description: The odd-kick value of the period-2 oscillating bipartite linear entropy.

linear_entropy_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of bipartite linear entropy.

expected_output.experiment_description: Numerical Floquet simulation of the same two-rotor kicked-rotor potential V(theta_1,theta_2)=k_1 cos(theta_1)+k_2 cos(theta_2)+xi cos(theta_1-theta_2), now with k_1=2, k_2=3, and xi=0.1. Both rotors are tuned to the secondary quantum resonance tau_1=tau_2=2*pi, with hbar=T=1. The initial state is |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>, and the entanglement bipartition is rotor 1 versus rotor 2 with linear entropy S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2). The wavepacket variances <p_1^2(t)> and <p_2^2(t)> and the linear entropy are evaluated over integer kick steps up to t=1000. This setup tests the central claim that when both rotors undergo the partial π translation, the single-rotor effective potentials have mixed symmetry while the inter-rotor coupling is symmetric, producing mixed wavepacket spreading but initially quadratic entanglement growth before saturation.

p1_variance_quadratic_coefficient_lambda.description: The coefficient of the quadratic component of the rotor-1 momentum variance.

p2_variance_quadratic_coefficient_lambda.description: The coefficient of the quadratic component of the rotor-2 momentum variance.

p1_variance_odd_step_oscillation_magnitu.description: The odd-step oscillation magnitude of the rotor-1 momentum variance.

p2_variance_odd_step_oscillation_magnitu.description: The odd-step oscillation magnitude of the rotor-2 momentum variance.

p1_wavepacket_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of the rotor-1 wavepacket variance.

p2_wavepacket_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of the rotor-2 wavepacket variance.

short_time_linear_entropy_quadratic_coef.description: The coefficient multiplying t squared in the short-time bipartite linear entropy.

linear_entropy_crossover_time_steps.description: The predicted crossover kick number separating early quadratic entanglement growth from saturation.

linear_entropy_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of bipartite linear entropy.

expected_output.experiment_description: Numerical Floquet simulation of a symmetry-broken variant of the two-rotor kicked-rotor model. The baseline potential is V(theta_1,theta_2)=k_1 cos(theta_1)+k_2 cos(theta_2)+xi cos(theta_1-theta_2) with k_1=2, k_2=3, and xi=0.1, and an additional inter-rotor term cos(2*theta_1-theta_2) is included in the kicking potential. Both rotors are at the secondary resonance tau_1=tau_2=2*pi, with hbar=T=1. The initial state is |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>, the bipartition is rotor 1 versus rotor 2, and S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2) is evaluated for kick steps up to t=1000. The setup targets the paper's central mixed-symmetry mechanism by adding an interaction component that is neither purely symmetric nor purely antisymmetric under the partial π translation.

linear_entropy_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of bipartite linear entropy under the added symmetry-breaking interaction.

expected_output.experiment_description: Numerical Floquet simulation of an extended two-rotor kicked-rotor model containing higher angular harmonics, used to test that the central symmetry mechanism does not depend on the specific low-harmonic potential form. The kicking potential is V(theta_1,theta_2)=k_1 cos(2*theta_1)+k_2 cos(2*theta_2)+xi cos(2*theta_1-theta_2), with k_1=k_2=0.1 and xi=1. Both rotors are tuned to the secondary resonance tau_1=tau_2=2*pi, hbar=T=1, and the initial state is |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>. The bipartition for entanglement is rotor 1 versus rotor 2, and linear entropy is S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2). The simulation evaluates <p_1^2(t)> and <p_2^2(t)> up to t=100 and S_lin(t) up to t=100. Under the partial π translation, the coupling term is antisymmetric while each rotor effective potential is mixed-symmetry, so the setup targets simultaneous hybrid wavepacket spreading and period-2 entanglement dynamics.

p1_variance_quadratic_coefficient_lambda.description: The coefficient of the quadratic component of the rotor-1 momentum variance.

p2_variance_quadratic_coefficient_lambda.description: The coefficient of the quadratic component of the rotor-2 momentum variance.

p1_variance_odd_step_oscillation_magnitu.description: The odd-step oscillation magnitude of the rotor-1 momentum variance.

p2_variance_odd_step_oscillation_magnitu.description: The odd-step oscillation magnitude of the rotor-2 momentum variance.

p1_wavepacket_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of the rotor-1 wavepacket variance.

p2_wavepacket_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of the rotor-2 wavepacket variance.

odd_step_linear_entropy.description: The odd-kick value of the period-2 oscillating bipartite linear entropy.

linear_entropy_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of bipartite linear entropy.

expected_output.experiment_description: Numerical Floquet simulations of higher-order-resonance two-rotor kicked-rotor models without imposing the special translational potential symmetry needed for the analytic high-order solution. The potential is V(theta_1,theta_2)=k_1 cos(theta_1)+k_2 cos(theta_2)+xi cos(theta_1-theta_2), with k_1=9, k_2=10, and xi=0.1. The initial state is |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>, hbar=T=1, and the bipartition is rotor 1 versus rotor 2 with linear entropy S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2). Three resonance-order pairs are simulated: tau_1=4*pi/3 with tau_2=4*pi/5, tau_1=4*pi/13 with tau_2=4*pi/15, and tau_1=4*pi/19 with tau_2=4*pi/21. The time sweep covers integer kicks up to t=1000. This setup characterizes how the central quantum-resonance wavepacket mechanism persists while entanglement changes when wavepacket splitting, proliferation, and interference occur in higher-order resonances.

p1_variance_time_exponent.description: The power-law exponent of the rotor-1 momentum variance growth versus kick number in the simulated higher-order resonances.

p2_variance_time_exponent.description: The power-law exponent of the rotor-2 momentum variance growth versus kick number in the simulated higher-order resonances.

linear_entropy_initial_time_exponent.description: The power-law exponent of the initial bipartite linear entropy growth before saturation in the simulated higher-order resonances.

linear_entropy_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of bipartite linear entropy for the high-order-resonance simulations.

expected_output.experiment_description: Robustness numerical simulations for the central resonance-controlled dynamics under weak detuning away from exact quantum resonance. The two-rotor potential is V(theta_1,theta_2)=k_1 cos(theta_1)+k_2 cos(theta_2)+xi cos(theta_1-theta_2), with k_1=2, k_2=3, and xi=0.1. The exact-resonance reference has rotor 1 at tau_1=4*pi and rotor 2 at tau_2=2*pi; detuned simulations use tau_1=4*pi+delta_tau_1 and tau_2=2*pi+delta_tau_2, where the offsets are incommensurate with 4*pi. The initial state is |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>, hbar=T=1, and linear entropy is computed for the rotor-1/rotor-2 bipartition. For the direct comparison, delta_tau_1=delta_tau_2=10^-3 and <p_1^2(t)>, <p_2^2(t)>, and S_lin(t) are compared to the exact-resonance trajectories up to t=100. For the scaling analysis, delta_tau_1=delta_tau_2=delta_tau is swept over 10^-3, 5*10^-4, 10^-4, 5*10^-5, and 10^-5. The deviation measure is Delta_1=|<p_1^2>_0-<p_1^2>|/<p_1^2>_0, where <p_1^2>_0 is the exact-resonance value. The agreement time t_D is defined as the kick number at which Delta_1 reaches a 1% threshold.

agreement_time_steps_for_delta_tau_1e_mi.description: The approximate kick number up to which the detuned and exact-resonance trajectories remain in agreement for equal detunings of 10^-3.

relative_deviation_time_exponent.description: The power-law exponent of the time growth of the rotor-1 relative deviation over the early detuning-sensitive interval.

agreement_time_detuning_scaling_exponent.description: The fitted exponent relating the 1% agreement time to equal detuning strength.

undetuned_odd_step_linear_entropy.description: The odd-kick value of the exact-resonance period-2 bipartite linear entropy for the reference system.

expected_output.experiment_description: Numerical simulation of the many-body kicked-top counterpart introduced to test whether the kicked-rotor central mechanism transfers to finite spherical phase space. The model contains two quantum tops with total angular momentum quantum number j_tot=50. The kick operator is U_k=exp[-i sum_{n=1}^2 beta_n J_{nz}^2/(2*j_tot)], and the between-kick Hamiltonian is H_f=alpha_1 J_{1x}+alpha_2 J_{2x}+(alpha_12/j_tot) J_{1x}J_{2x}+(alpha_122/j_tot^2) J_{1x}J_{2x}^2. The parameters are alpha_1=0.0001, alpha_2=0.02, alpha_12=0.005, and alpha_122=0.0005. Top 1 is at the principal kicked-top resonance beta_1=4*pi*j_tot, and top 2 is at the secondary resonance beta_2=2*pi*j_tot. The initial state is |J_{1z}=0> tensor |J_{2z}=0>. The bipartition is top 1 versus top 2, and linear entropy is S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2). The simulation tracks the normalized variances <J_{1z}^2>/j_tot^2 and <J_{2z}^2>/j_tot^2 and S_lin over kick numbers up to about 10^4. The setup targets the kicked-top analogue of the mixed-symmetry resonance mechanism, while accounting for the finite spherical phase-space bound on wavepacket spreading.

j1z_wavepacket_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of the top-1 angular-momentum variance before finite-phase-space saturation.

j2z_wavepacket_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of the top-2 angular-momentum variance before finite-phase-space saturation.

linear_entropy_dynamical_regime.description: The classified dynamical regime of bipartite linear entropy in the kicked-top simulation.

wavepacket_variance_saturation_scale_for.description: The finite spherical phase-space scale at which kicked-top wavepacket variance ceases unbounded growth.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Numerical Floquet simulation of the two-rotor kicked-rotor model used to illustrate the paper's symmetry-selection mechanism connecting wavepacket spreading and entanglement. The kicking potential is V(theta_1,theta_2)=k_1 cos(theta_1)+k_2 cos(theta_2)+xi cos(theta_1-theta_2), with k_1=0.1, k_2=0.2, and xi=1. Rotor 1 is set at the principal quantum resonance tau_1=4*pi and rotor 2 at the secondary quantum resonance tau_2=2*pi; hbar=T=1. The initial state is the product momentum eigenstate |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>. The bipartition for entanglement is rotor 1 versus rotor 2, and linear entropy is S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2). The simulation evaluates <p_1^2(t)> over kick steps shown on a logarithmic time axis up to t=1000, and <p_2^2(t)> and S_lin(t) over kick steps up to t=100. The central concept tested is that the partial π translation of the secondary-resonant rotor makes the rotor-1 effective potential mixed-symmetry, the rotor-2 effective potential antisymmetric, and the inter-rotor coupling antisymmetric, so the measured quantities target hybrid, anti-resonant, and entanglement-oscillatory responses respectively.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Numerical Floquet simulation of the same two-rotor kicked-rotor potential V(theta_1,theta_2)=k_1 cos(theta_1)+k_2 cos(theta_2)+xi cos(theta_1-theta_2), now with k_1=2, k_2=3, and xi=0.1. Both rotors are tuned to the secondary quantum resonance tau_1=tau_2=2*pi, with hbar=T=1. The initial state is |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>, and the entanglement bipartition is rotor 1 versus rotor 2 with linear entropy S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2). The wavepacket variances <p_1^2(t)> and <p_2^2(t)> and the linear entropy are evaluated over integer kick steps up to t=1000. This setup tests the central claim that when both rotors undergo the partial π translation, the single-rotor effective potentials have mixed symmetry while the inter-rotor coupling is symmetric, producing mixed wavepacket spreading but initially quadratic entanglement growth before saturation.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Numerical Floquet simulation of a symmetry-broken variant of the two-rotor kicked-rotor model. The baseline potential is V(theta_1,theta_2)=k_1 cos(theta_1)+k_2 cos(theta_2)+xi cos(theta_1-theta_2) with k_1=2, k_2=3, and xi=0.1, and an additional inter-rotor term cos(2*theta_1-theta_2) is included in the kicking potential. Both rotors are at the secondary resonance tau_1=tau_2=2*pi, with hbar=T=1. The initial state is |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>, the bipartition is rotor 1 versus rotor 2, and S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2) is evaluated for kick steps up to t=1000. The setup targets the paper's central mixed-symmetry mechanism by adding an interaction component that is neither purely symmetric nor purely antisymmetric under the partial π translation.

Both rotors are tuned to the secondary resonance tau_1=tau_2=2*pi, hbar=T=1, and the initial state is |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>. The bipartition for entanglement is rotor 1 versus rotor 2, and linear entropy is S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2). The simulation evaluates <p_1^2(t)> and <p_2^2(t)> up to t=100 and S_lin(t) up to t=100. Under the partial π translation, the coupling term is antisymmetric while each rotor effective potential is mixed-symmetry, so the setup targets simultaneous hybrid wavepacket spreading and period-2 entanglement dynamics.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Numerical Floquet simulations of higher-order-resonance two-rotor kicked-rotor models without imposing the special translational potential symmetry needed for the analytic high-order solution. The potential is V(theta_1,theta_2)=k_1 cos(theta_1)+k_2 cos(theta_2)+xi cos(theta_1-theta_2), with k_1=9, k_2=10, and xi=0.1. The initial state is |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>, hbar=T=1, and the bipartition is rotor 1 versus rotor 2 with linear entropy S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2). Three resonance-order pairs are simulated: tau_1=4*pi/3 with tau_2=4*pi/5, tau_1=4*pi/13 with tau_2=4*pi/15, and tau_1=4*pi/19 with tau_2=4*pi/21. The time sweep covers integer kicks up to t=1000. This setup characterizes how the central quantum-resonance wavepacket mechanism persists while entanglement changes when wavepacket splitting, proliferation, and interference occur in higher-order resonances.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Robustness numerical simulations for the central resonance-controlled dynamics under weak detuning away from exact quantum resonance. The two-rotor potential is V(theta_1,theta_2)=k_1 cos(theta_1)+k_2 cos(theta_2)+xi cos(theta_1-theta_2), with k_1=2, k_2=3, and xi=0.1. The exact-resonance reference has rotor 1 at tau_1=4*pi and rotor 2 at tau_2=2*pi; detuned simulations use tau_1=4*pi+delta_tau_1 and tau_2=2*pi+delta_tau_2, where the offsets are incommensurate with 4*pi. The initial state is |p_1=0> tensor |p_2=0>, hbar=T=1, and linear entropy is computed for the rotor-1/rotor-2 bipartition. For the direct comparison, delta_tau_1=delta_tau_2=10^-3 and <p_1^2(t)>, <p_2^2(t)>, and S_lin(t) are compared to the exact-resonance trajectories up to t=100. For the scaling analysis, delta_tau_1=delta_tau_2=delta_tau is swept over 10^-3, 5*10^-4, 10^-4, 5*10^-5, and 10^-5. The deviation measure is Delta_1=|<p_1^2>_0-<p_1^2>|/<p_1^2>_0, where <p_1^2>_0 is the exact-resonance value. The agreement time t_D is defined as the kick number at which Delta_1 reaches a 1% threshold.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Numerical simulation of the many-body kicked-top counterpart introduced to test whether the kicked-rotor central mechanism transfers to finite spherical phase space. The model contains two quantum tops with total angular momentum quantum number j_tot=50. The kick operator is U_k=exp[-i sum_{n=1}^2 beta_n J_{nz}^2/(2*j_tot)], and the between-kick Hamiltonian is H_f=alpha_1 J_{1x}+alpha_2 J_{2x}+(alpha_12/j_tot) J_{1x}J_{2x}+(alpha_122/j_tot^2) J_{1x}J_{2x}^2. The parameters are alpha_1=0.0001, alpha_2=0.02, alpha_12=0.005, and alpha_122=0.0005. Top 1 is at the principal kicked-top resonance beta_1=4*pi*j_tot, and top 2 is at the secondary resonance beta_2=2*pi*j_tot. The initial state is |J_{1z}=0> tensor |J_{2z}=0>. The bipartition is top 1 versus top 2, and linear entropy is S_lin=1-Tr(rho_1^2). The simulation tracks the normalized variances <J_{1z}^2>/j_tot^2 and <J_{2z}^2>/j_tot^2 and S_lin over kick numbers up to about 10^4. The setup targets the kicked-top analogue of the mixed-symmetry resonance mechanism, while accounting for the finite spherical phase-space bound on wavepacket spreading.

per_file.paper_title: Wave–particle transition and quantum Zeno effect in which-way experiments with a superconducting quantum processor

expected_output.experiment_description: Four-qubit superconducting-qubit Mach–Zehnder interferometry experiment configured to test a tunable wave-to-particle transition under pulsed which-way measurement. The active interferometer is the Q0–Q1–Q2–Q3 plaquette of a 4×4 frequency-tunable transmon array: Q0 acts as the first beam splitter, Q1 is path 1, Q2 is path 2 and the monitored which-way site, and Q3 acts as the second beam splitter and output port. All four qubits are initially measured and post-selected in |0>. A microwave photon is generated by applying a π pulse to Q0. Q0, Q1, and Q2 are tuned by Z pulses to the common working frequency 5.82 GHz for 57 ns to split the excitation between Q1 and Q2. The arms are then decoupled by biasing Q0 to its idle frequency, keeping Q2 at 5.82 GHz, and biasing Q1 to the waiting frequency 5.83 GHz. A 100 ns dispersive readout pulse is applied to Q2’s readout resonator as the which-way measurement, followed by a 100 ns resonator-decay wait. The calibrated average measurement-induced dephasing strength Γm/2π is swept from 0 to 3.695 MHz. A controllable phase is applied on path 1 by biasing Q1 to 5.83 GHz + δ/2π for tp = 100 ns, with δ/2π swept from 0 to 30 MHz so that the phase is phi = -tp δ. Q1, Q2, and Q3 are then tuned to 5.82 GHz for 49 ns to recombine the two paths at Q3. The Q3 excited-state population PI is measured as a function of δ and fit to a sinusoidal interference fringe. Visibility is defined as V = (PImax - PImin)/(PImax + PImin), where PImax and PImin are the fitted maximum and minimum Q3 populations over the δ sweep. The geometric scope is the entire four-qubit interferometer plaquette; the measurement compares the same output port Q3 across the full phase sweep for each calibrated Γm.

expected_output.experiment_description: Two-qubit quantum-state tomography experiment on the two arms of the 4-qubit superconducting-qubit Mach–Zehnder interferometer, configured to quantify how pulsed which-way measurement transfers information from the path qubits to the measurement apparatus. The active interferometer region is the same Q0–Q1–Q2–Q3 plaquette, with Q1 and Q2 representing the two arms after the first beam splitter. The preparation and first beamsplitting stage are identical to the 4-qubit interference experiment: all qubits are initially read out and post-selected in |0>, Q0 is excited by a π pulse, and Q0, Q1, and Q2 are tuned to 5.82 GHz for 57 ns. The qubits are then decoupled, and a 100 ns dispersive which-way readout pulse with calibrated average dephasing Γm is applied to Q2’s readout resonator. The Γm/2π sweep covers 0 to 3.695 MHz. Instead of applying the phase-scan and recombination steps, the circuit waits with Q1 and Q2 decoupled and then performs two-qubit tomography on Q1 and Q2. From the reconstructed density matrix rho_Q1Q2, the concurrence is computed using the Wootters definition C = max(0, λ1 - λ2 - λ3 - λ4), where λi are the square roots of the eigenvalues of rho rho_tilde in decreasing order and rho_tilde = (sigma_y ⊗ sigma_y) rho* (sigma_y ⊗ sigma_y). The single-excitation density matrix is rho_s = P rho_Q1Q2 P / Tr(P rho_Q1Q2), with P = |10><10| + |01><01|. The purity is Ps = Tr(rho_s^2), and the von Neumann entropy is Ss = -Tr(rho_s log2 rho_s). The spatial-geometric scope is the two arm qubits Q1 and Q2, measured jointly after the controlled path-splitting and which-way pulse.

expected_output.experiment_description: Twelve-qubit superconducting-qubit Mach–Zehnder interferometry experiment configured to test continuous which-way monitoring and quantum-Zeno backaction during coherent propagation. The active interferometer is embedded in the 4×4 transmon processor and uses 12 qubits. Q0 is the initial beam splitter; path 1 is Q1, Q4, Q5, Q7, and Q13; path 2 is Q2, Q8, Q10, Q11, and Q14; Q15 is the final beam splitter/output region. All participating qubits are initially biased to idle frequencies and measured for initial-state post-selection. A microwave photon is generated by exciting Q0. The 12 interferometer qubits are then tuned to the common working frequency 5.82 GHz for coherent evolution over a time window from 0 to 200 ns. The central mechanism tested is that continuous dispersive monitoring of Q2, a site at the entrance to path 2, can both provide which-way information and alter transport by quantum-Zeno reflection when the measurement-induced dephasing rate becomes comparable to or exceeds the Q0–Q2 hopping scale. The which-way measurement pulse on Q2’s readout resonator is started before initial state preparation so that its strength is stabilized when the joint evolution begins, maintained throughout the 12-qubit evolution, and accompanied by a Z-bias compensation for the measurement-induced Stark shift. Γm/2π is set to calibrated values including 0, 5.921, 11.195, and 18.134 MHz. At each evolution time, the qubit populations <n_i> are obtained by simultaneous projective readout of the 12 active sites. The spatial-geometric scope is the complete 12-site interferometer, with population dynamics compared along both arms and at Q15 over the full 0–200 ns evolution window.

expected_output.experiment_description: Two-qubit tomography experiment on the two arms of the continuously monitored 12-qubit superconducting-qubit Mach–Zehnder interferometer, configured to quantify quantum-information leakage and its modification by quantum-Zeno backaction. The active device and interferometer geometry are the 12-site Q0-to-Q15 Mach–Zehnder network on the 4×4 transmon processor: path 1 contains Q1, Q4, Q5, Q7, and Q13, while path 2 contains Q2, Q8, Q10, Q11, and Q14. The monitored which-way site is Q2. Initial-state post-selection, Q0 excitation, tuning of all interferometer qubits to 5.82 GHz, and continuous Q2 dispersive measurement are performed as in the 12-qubit population-dynamics experiment. The calibrated continuous measurement-induced dephasing Γm/2π is swept over the plotted range from 0 to about 24 MHz. Two-qubit tomography is performed on Q4 and Q8, one qubit on each arm downstream of the monitored entrance region, at the fixed evolution time corresponding to the maximum Q4–Q8 concurrence in the absence of the which-way measurement. From the reconstructed rho_Q4Q8, concurrence CQ4Q8 is computed using the Wootters definition. The single-excitation subspace density matrix is formed with P = |10><10| + |01><01| as rho_s = P rho_Q4Q8 P / Tr(P rho_Q4Q8), with purity Ps = Tr(rho_s^2) and von Neumann entropy Ss = -Tr(rho_s log2 rho_s). The spatial-geometric scope is the paired downstream arm sites Q4 and Q8, sampled as a function of the continuously monitored Q2 measurement strength.

From the reconstructed density matrix rho_Q1Q2, the concurrence is computed using the Wootters definition C = max(0, λ1 - λ2 - λ3 - λ4), where λi are the square roots of the eigenvalues of rho rho_tilde in decreasing order and rho_tilde = (sigma_y ⊗ sigma_y) rho* (sigma_y ⊗ sigma_y). The single-excitation density matrix is rho_s = P rho_Q1Q2 P / Tr(P rho_Q1Q2), with P = |10><10| + |01><01|. The purity is Ps = Tr(rho_s^2), and the von Neumann entropy is Ss = -Tr(rho_s log2 rho_s). The spatial-geometric scope is the two arm qubits Q1 and Q2, measured jointly after the controlled path-splitting and which-way pulse.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Twelve-qubit superconducting-qubit Mach–Zehnder interferometry experiment configured to test continuous which-way monitoring and quantum-Zeno backaction during coherent propagation. The active interferometer is embedded in the 4×4 transmon processor and uses 12 qubits. Q0 is the initial beam splitter; path 1 is Q1, Q4, Q5, Q7, and Q13; path 2 is Q2, Q8, Q10, Q11, and Q14; Q15 is the final beam splitter/output region. All participating qubits are initially biased to idle frequencies and measured for initial-state post-selection. A microwave photon is generated by exciting Q0. The 12 interferometer qubits are then tuned to the common working frequency 5.82 GHz for coherent evolution over a time window from 0 to 200 ns. The central mechanism tested is that continuous dispersive monitoring of Q2, a site at the entrance to path 2, can both provide which-way information and alter transport by quantum-Zeno reflection when the measurement-induced dephasing rate becomes comparable to or exceeds the Q0–Q2 hopping scale. The which-way measurement pulse on Q2’s readout resonator is started before initial state preparation so that its strength is stabilized when the joint evolution begins, maintained throughout the 12-qubit evolution, and accompanied by a Z-bias compensation for the measurement-induced Stark shift. Γm/2π is set to calibrated values including 0, 5.921, 11.195, and 18.134 MHz. At each evolution time, the qubit populations <n_i> are obtained by simultaneous projective readout of the 12 active sites. The spatial-geometric scope is the complete 12-site interferometer, with population dynamics compared along both arms and at Q15 over the full 0–200 ns evolution window.

Initial-state post-selection, Q0 excitation, tuning of all interferometer qubits to 5.82 GHz, and continuous Q2 dispersive measurement are performed as in the 12-qubit population-dynamics experiment. The calibrated continuous measurement-induced dephasing Γm/2π is swept over the plotted range from 0 to about 24 MHz. per_file.paper_title: Enhanced Atom Capture via Multi-Frequency Magneto-Optical Trapping

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: implement a practical multi-frequency 87Rb magneto-optical trap (MOT) in which additional red-detuned cooling frequencies are confined primarily to an annular beam surrounding the trapped cloud, so that incident thermal atoms can be slowed over a wider Doppler range while minimizing overlap of far-red cooling light with already trapped atoms. The optical-field generation procedure uses a double-passed acousto-optic modulator driven simultaneously with multiple radio-frequency tones; a lens places the retroreflecting mirror in a geometry that recombines the different AOM deflection angles into one spatially overlapped beam, and a tapered amplifier boosts the resulting multi-frequency output. A second AOM partially cancels the large carrier frequency shift so that the optical components lie at the desired detunings relative to the 87Rb D2 F=2 to F'=3 cooling transition. The resulting multi-frequency beam is transformed from an initially Gaussian beam into an annular cooling beam with a pair of axicon lenses, with an upstream iris controlling the central hole. The conventional trapping light is a Gaussian component near the usual MOT detuning, while the additional cooling components are intended to be further red-detuned and present only in the axicon-produced ring beam. Characterization consists of measuring the optical frequency spectrum with a Fabry–Perot interferometric analyzer over the relevant detuning range relative to the F=2 to F'=3 transition, and imaging the transverse cooling-beam intensity profile across the full beam cross-section after the axicon pair. The spatial characterization targets the entire transverse annular beam profile over the MOT-beam scale; the paper reports a normalized cross-section through the profile but does not report averaging over multiple beam locations or repeated assemblies.

single_sided_red_detuned_multifrequency_.description: Whether the optical generation procedure produced a spectrum with multiple cooling components on the red-detuned side of the 87Rb cooling transition rather than a symmetric phase-modulation spectrum.

annular_cooling_beam_profile_produced.description: Whether the axicon-lens beam-shaping procedure produced the intended hollow annular transverse cooling-beam geometry for the multi-frequency light.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: map the atom-capture landscape of a dual-frequency version of the 87Rb MOT to distinguish frequency regimes associated with enhanced loading. The apparatus is a six-beam vapor-cell 87Rb magneto-optical trap without additional Zeeman slower, 2D-MOT source, or atomic beam slowing stage. The measurement uses two cooling optical frequencies near the 87Rb D2 F=2 to F'=3 transition and records the number of atoms loaded after a fixed 5 s MOT loading time while sweeping both the fundamental cooler detuning and the frequency difference between the two cooling components. The plotted scan covers fundamental cooler detunings from approximately -15 MHz to -20 MHz relative to the cooling transition and dual-frequency spacings from 0 MHz to about 25 MHz. Atom number is obtained by absorption imaging: after switching off cooling/trapping beams and magnetic field, an approximately 35 microsecond probe pulse resonant with F=2 to F'=3 is applied after an approximately 15 ms fall time; the optical-depth image is fit to a two-dimensional Gaussian and rescaled to account for the cloud extending beyond the imaging-beam field of view, then integrated over the whole MOT cloud. The scan probes the full trapped cloud at the six-beam intersection for each frequency setting; the paper presents an interpolated surface over the swept parameter plane and does not report independent spatial subregions within the cloud.

dual_frequency_loading_trough_spacing_MH.description: The frequency spacing between the two cooling components at which the atom-number landscape contains a pronounced loading trough.

global_enhancement_regime_frequency_spac.description: The dual-frequency spacing associated with the global enhanced-loading regime in the atom-number landscape.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: compare a conventional single-frequency 87Rb MOT with the proposed multi-frequency MOT, where additional red-detuned cooling components are applied in an annular axicon beam to increase capture velocity from a thermal background while avoiding strong overlap with the trapped cloud. The MOT uses three orthogonal pairs of counter-propagating, non-retroreflected beams. The conventional Gaussian trapping beams have diameter about 38 mm, 1/e^2 radius approximately 15 mm, are truncated at about 19 mm radius, and contain cooling light detuned near -20 MHz from the 87Rb D2 F=2 to F'=3 transition plus repumper light resonant with F=1 to F'=2. Typical per-beam powers are about 20 mW in the trapping light and about 18 mW in the repumper. The multi-frequency condition adds an overlapping axicon-generated annular cooling beam containing about five additional further red-detuned optical components spanning approximately -25 MHz to -45 MHz from F=2 to F'=3, with typical cooling power about 45 mW per beam. Anti-Helmholtz coils provide the MOT quadrupole magnetic field, and the axial magnetic-field gradient is swept over the experimentally accessible range up to about 22 G cm^-1. For each magnetic-field-gradient setting and each optical configuration, MOT load time is varied; at the end of loading an approximately 20 ms interval with only single-frequency trapping light is applied before imaging. Absorption imaging uses an approximately 35 microsecond resonant F=2 to F'=3 probe after about 15 ms free fall, and the complete cloud optical-depth projection is fit to a two-dimensional Gaussian, rescaled to the physical cloud extent, and integrated. Each reported loading rate R and steady-state atom number N_ss is extracted from a fit of the whole-cloud atom number versus load time to N = R*tau*(1 - exp(-t/tau)), where N is atom number, R is the MOT loading rate, tau is the characteristic MOT loading time, and t is the MOT load time; a time-axis offset is allowed in the fit to account for shutter timing. The spatial scope is the entire trapped atom cloud at the beam intersection for each load curve; the paper does not report atom-number averages over separate cloud subregions, but each data point comes from a load-time scan under fixed beam and field conditions.

per_file.paper_title: Observation antibunching with classical light in a linear interferometer

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept tested: a modified Hanbury Brown–Twiss interferometer is used to determine whether classical pseudothermal light can exhibit one-zero photon-number-projection antibunching when ordinary single-photon detectors are treated as photon-number-resolving detectors by binning their time-tagged outputs. A single-mode continuous-wave laser at 780 nm center wavelength with 200 kHz frequency bandwidth is incident on a rotating ground glass to generate pseudothermal light; the laser intensity is adjusted with a variable light-intensity attenuator, and the laser spot size on the rotating ground glass is controlled by the lens-to-ground-glass distance. The scattered light is split by a 1:1 non-polarizing beam splitter. Two single-mode-fiber couplers with 4.0 µm core-diameter fibers define the two detection modes and send light to two single-photon detectors D1 and D2. The fiber couplers are placed at symmetric output positions of the beamsplitter for the temporal measurement, with no spatial scan. Photon arrival times from D1 and D2 are recorded on a common clock using a HydraHarp 400 photon detection time-series module, and the offline analysis bins the events into time bins of T = 1 µs. The D1 and D2 single-photon count rates used for this temporal data set are 734.57 kHz and 583.82 kHz, corresponding to 0.73 and 0.58 detected photons per bin and an averaged photon number per detector of \bar n = 0.66. For each integer m = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, the measured quantity is g_m0^(2)(τ), the normalized correlation between the event “D1 detects m photons in a bin” and “D2 detects zero photons in a bin,” normalized by the corresponding marginal probabilities; τ is the relative delay between detector time bins. per_file.paper_title: Direct Time-Domain Observation of l-Doubling via Centrifugal-Distortion Pre-compensation

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept tested: a femtosecond pump pulse with a tailored cubic spectral phase is used to imprint a Raman-coherence phase that cancels centrifugal-distortion dephasing at a chosen rotational revival of a gas-phase molecular rotor. The validation target is methyl iodide (CH3I), a symmetric-top molecule with strong centrifugal distortion and no l-doubling contribution in the alignment signal. CH3I gas is held at 15 torr and room temperature in the spectroscopic gas cell. A Ti:sapphire/CPA ultrafast source provides approximately 800 nm, 110–120 fs pulses. The beam is split into a strong pump arm carrying about 90% of the energy and a weak probe arm carrying about 10%. The pump is sent through a 4-f pulse shaper consisting of two gratings, cylindrical reflective optics, and a Jenoptik dual-mask 640-pixel spatial light modulator located at the Fourier plane. The probe is frequency doubled in a BBO crystal to 400 nm. Pump and probe propagate collinearly through the gas; the birefringence measurement integrates over the pump–probe overlap volume along the gas-cell path, with no spatial scan or lateral/depth-resolved imaging reported. The probe polarization is set to 45 degrees relative to the pump polarization; after the cell the transmitted probe passes through a quarter-wave plate and Wollaston prism and is read by balanced photodetectors to record transient optical birefringence versus pump–probe delay. Reference traces use an unshaped transform-limited near-IR pump. Shaped traces use a spectral phase Phi_shape(omega)=a_tilde(omega-omega0)^2+b_tilde(omega-omega0)^3, where omega is optical angular frequency, omega0 is the pump carrier angular frequency, a_tilde is the quadratic spectral-phase coefficient, and b_tilde is the cubic spectral-phase coefficient. For the analytic cubic-phase design, a_tilde is set to zero and b_tilde is chosen for a target revival order n using the molecular rotational constant B and centrifugal-distortion constant D in consistent spectroscopic units; T_rev=(2Bc)^(-1), with c the speed of light. The reported CH3I constants used for the design context are B=0.25 cm^-1 and D=2.1e-7 cm^-1. Time-domain windows are examined around the 1.5 T_rev, 2.5 T_rev, and 5.5 T_rev fractional revivals. The applied cubic phase coefficients are b_tilde=2.0e7 fs^3 for 1.5 T_rev, b_tilde=3.4e7 fs^3 for 2.5 T_rev, and b_tilde=6.8e7 fs^3 for 5.5 T_rev. The time axis is referenced by setting the first signal peak at the end of the excitation pulse to t=0. The measurement is configured to compare the revival waveform morphology under unshaped excitation with the waveform obtained when the cubic phase is selected to pre-compensate centrifugal distortion at the chosen delay.

analytic_vs_numerical_cubic_phase_differ.description: Upper bound on the reported difference between the analytic cubic-phase approximation and brute-force least-squares numerical optimization for revival orders greater than five.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept tested: before applying centrifugal-distortion pre-compensation to resolve closely spaced l-doubling contributions in carbon dioxide, the time-domain width of a conventional CO2 alignment feature is measured to set the temporal scale required for separating different rotational-vibrational components. CO2 gas is measured by time-resolved optical birefringence in the same collinear pump–probe geometry: an approximately 800 nm, 120 fs transform-limited pump excites rotational Raman coherences; a weak 400 nm probe generated by frequency doubling in BBO crosses the same gas volume collinearly; the probe polarization is 45 degrees relative to the pump; a quarter-wave plate, Wollaston prism, and balanced photodetectors analyze the transmitted probe polarization. The measurement integrates over the pump–probe overlap volume in the gas cell; no spatial scan, imaging resolution, or transverse homogeneity map is reported. The pump is unshaped for this reference measurement. The pump–probe delay is scanned around the CO2 three-quarter revival, 3/4 T_rev, using the CO2 rotational timing context given by the B000 ground-state rotational constant. The gas pressure is not specified in the provided text. The measurement is configured to determine the temporal duration of the short-delay alignment transient used as a reference for evaluating resolvability of l-doubling-related alignment events at later revivals.

co2_reference_alignment_signal_duration_.description: Temporal duration of the short-delay CO2 alignment feature measured under transform-limited excitation.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept tested: in CO2, l-doubling in the v=1 bending manifold gives multiple rotational-wavepacket contributions with slightly different revival periods, but conventional impulsive alignment can leave those contributions overlapped at long delay because centrifugal distortion broadens the revival waveforms. CO2 gas is placed in the heated spectroscopic cell and measured by collinear time-resolved optical birefringence. An approximately 800 nm, 120 fs transform-limited pump pulse excites rotational alignment without spectral phase shaping. A weak probe arm is frequency doubled in BBO to 400 nm and read out after the sample using 45-degree probe polarization, a quarter-wave plate, a Wollaston prism, and balanced photodetection. The measurement integrates over the pump–probe overlap volume along the cell; no spatially resolved scan or gas-density homogeneity map is reported. The gas is heated to 403 K to increase the thermal population of the v=1 bending manifold associated with l-doubling, while also sampling a higher-J rotational distribution. The CO2 rotational constants used as timing context are B000=0.3902 cm^-1, B010+=0.3912 cm^-1, and B010-=0.3905 cm^-1, with centrifugal-distortion constant D=1.33e-7 cm^-1. The pump–probe delay is scanned near the long-delay 32 T_rev region, around 1380 ps after excitation, where the l-doubling-related revival events are expected to be separated in arrival time by the small differences in rotational constants. The measurement is configured to determine whether the separate rotational-vibrational alignment contributions can be distinguished without centrifugal-distortion pre-compensation.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept tested: a cubic spectral phase applied to the femtosecond pump pulse is used to pre-compensate centrifugal-distortion dephasing in CO2 at a long-delay revival so that l-doubling-related rotational-vibrational contributions can be directly observed in the time domain. CO2 gas is measured in the heated-cell transient-birefringence apparatus using collinear pump and probe beams. The pump is an approximately 800 nm, 120 fs near-IR pulse routed through the 4-f pulse shaper with gratings, cylindrical reflective optics, and a Jenoptik dual-mask 640-pixel spatial light modulator; its spectral phase is selected according to the cubic pre-compensation design for the 32 T_rev region. The weak probe is generated at 400 nm by frequency doubling in BBO and analyzed after the gas with 45-degree input polarization, a quarter-wave plate, a Wollaston prism, and balanced photodetectors. The measurement integrates over the pump–probe overlap volume in the gas cell; no lateral scan, depth-resolved measurement, or transverse homogeneity assessment is reported. The CO2 pressure is not specified in the provided text. Measurements are taken at both 293 K and 403 K. Heating to 403 K is used as a controlled condition to increase the population of the v=1 bending mode at omega_bend=667 cm^-1. The timing analysis uses the CO2 rotational constants B000=0.3902 cm^-1, B010+=0.3912 cm^-1, and B010-=0.3905 cm^-1, corresponding to the ground vibrational state and the two l-doubled v=1 bending components. The pump–probe delay range recorded for the long-delay measurement is 1380–1412 ps, spanning alignment events around the 32 T_rev to 33 T_rev region. The plotted traces are normalized to the 32 3/4 T_rev revival of the ground-vibrational-level rotational constant B000. The measurement is configured to determine whether the centrifugal-distortion-precompensated response separates the ground-state and l-doubled bending-state contributions in time.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept tested: a femtosecond pump pulse with a tailored cubic spectral phase is used to imprint a Raman-coherence phase that cancels centrifugal-distortion dephasing at a chosen rotational revival of a gas-phase molecular rotor. The validation target is methyl iodide (CH3I), a symmetric-top molecule with strong centrifugal distortion and no l-doubling contribution in the alignment signal. CH3I gas is held at 15 torr and room temperature in the spectroscopic gas cell. A Ti:sapphire/CPA ultrafast source provides approximately 800 nm, 110–120 fs pulses. The beam is split into a strong pump arm carrying about 90% of the energy and a weak probe arm carrying about 10%. The pump is sent through a 4-f pulse shaper consisting of two gratings, cylindrical reflective optics, and a Jenoptik dual-mask 640-pixel spatial light modulator located at the Fourier plane. The probe is frequency doubled in a BBO crystal to 400 nm. Pump and probe propagate collinearly through the gas; the birefringence measurement integrates over the pump–probe overlap volume along the gas-cell path, with no spatial scan or lateral/depth-resolved imaging reported. The probe polarization is set to 45 degrees relative to the pump polarization; after the cell the transmitted probe passes through a quarter-wave plate and Wollaston prism and is read by balanced photodetectors to record transient optical birefringence versus pump–probe delay. Reference traces use an unshaped transform-limited near-IR pump. Shaped traces use a spectral phase Phi_shape(omega)=a_tilde(omega-omega0)^2+b_tilde(omega-omega0)^3, where omega is optical angular frequency, omega0 is the pump carrier angular frequency, a_tilde is the quadratic spectral-phase coefficient, and b_tilde is the cubic spectral-phase coefficient. For the analytic cubic-phase design, a_tilde is set to zero and b_tilde is chosen for a target revival order n using the molecular rotational constant B and centrifugal-distortion constant D in consistent spectroscopic units; T_rev=(2Bc)^(-1), with c the speed of light. The reported CH3I constants used for the design context are B=0.25 cm^-1 and D=2.1e-7 cm^-1. Time-domain windows are examined around the 1.5 T_rev, 2.5 T_rev, and 5.5 T_rev fractional revivals. The applied cubic phase coefficients are b_tilde=2.0e7 fs^3 for 1.5 T_rev, b_tilde=3.4e7 fs^3 for 2.5 T_rev, and b_tilde=6.8e7 fs^3 for 5.5 T_rev. The time axis is referenced by setting the first signal peak at the end of the excitation pulse to t=0. The measurement is configured to compare the revival waveform morphology under unshaped excitation with the waveform obtained when the cubic phase is selected to pre-compensate centrifugal distortion at the chosen delay.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept tested: before applying centrifugal-distortion pre-compensation to resolve closely spaced l-doubling contributions in carbon dioxide, the time-domain width of a conventional CO2 alignment feature is measured to set the temporal scale required for separating different rotational-vibrational components. CO2 gas is measured by time-resolved optical birefringence in the same collinear pump–probe geometry: an approximately 800 nm, 120 fs transform-limited pump excites rotational Raman coherences; a weak 400 nm probe generated by frequency doubling in BBO crosses the same gas volume collinearly; the probe polarization is 45 degrees relative to the pump; a quarter-wave plate, Wollaston prism, and balanced photodetectors analyze the transmitted probe polarization. The measurement integrates over the pump–probe overlap volume in the gas cell; no spatial scan, imaging resolution, or transverse homogeneity map is reported. The pump is unshaped for this reference measurement. The pump–probe delay is scanned around the CO2 three-quarter revival, 3/4 T_rev, using the CO2 rotational timing context given by the B000 ground-state rotational constant. The gas pressure is not specified in the provided text. The measurement is configured to determine the temporal duration of the short-delay alignment transient used as a reference for evaluating resolvability of l-doubling-related alignment events at later revivals.

result_rows.description: Temporal duration of the short-delay CO2 alignment feature measured under transform-limited excitation.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept tested: in CO2, l-doubling in the v=1 bending manifold gives multiple rotational-wavepacket contributions with slightly different revival periods, but conventional impulsive alignment can leave those contributions overlapped at long delay because centrifugal distortion broadens the revival waveforms. CO2 gas is placed in the heated spectroscopic cell and measured by collinear time-resolved optical birefringence. An approximately 800 nm, 120 fs transform-limited pump pulse excites rotational alignment without spectral phase shaping. A weak probe arm is frequency doubled in BBO to 400 nm and read out after the sample using 45-degree probe polarization, a quarter-wave plate, a Wollaston prism, and balanced photodetection. The measurement integrates over the pump–probe overlap volume along the cell; no spatially resolved scan or gas-density homogeneity map is reported. The gas is heated to 403 K to increase the thermal population of the v=1 bending manifold associated with l-doubling, while also sampling a higher-J rotational distribution. The CO2 rotational constants used as timing context are B000=0.3902 cm^-1, B010+=0.3912 cm^-1, and B010-=0.3905 cm^-1, with centrifugal-distortion constant D=1.33e-7 cm^-1. The pump–probe delay is scanned near the long-delay 32 T_rev region, around 1380 ps after excitation, where the l-doubling-related revival events are expected to be separated in arrival time by the small differences in rotational constants. The measurement is configured to determine whether the separate rotational-vibrational alignment contributions can be distinguished without centrifugal-distortion pre-compensation.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept tested: a cubic spectral phase applied to the femtosecond pump pulse is used to pre-compensate centrifugal-distortion dephasing in CO2 at a long-delay revival so that l-doubling-related rotational-vibrational contributions can be directly observed in the time domain. CO2 gas is measured in the heated-cell transient-birefringence apparatus using collinear pump and probe beams. The pump is an approximately 800 nm, 120 fs near-IR pulse routed through the 4-f pulse shaper with gratings, cylindrical reflective optics, and a Jenoptik dual-mask 640-pixel spatial light modulator; its spectral phase is selected according to the cubic pre-compensation design for the 32 T_rev region. The weak probe is generated at 400 nm by frequency doubling in BBO and analyzed after the gas with 45-degree input polarization, a quarter-wave plate, a Wollaston prism, and balanced photodetectors. The measurement integrates over the pump–probe overlap volume in the gas cell; no lateral scan, depth-resolved measurement, or transverse homogeneity assessment is reported. The CO2 pressure is not specified in the provided text. Measurements are taken at both 293 K and 403 K. Heating to 403 K is used as a controlled condition to increase the population of the v=1 bending mode at omega_bend=667 cm^-1. The timing analysis uses the CO2 rotational constants B000=0.3902 cm^-1, B010+=0.3912 cm^-1, and B010-=0.3905 cm^-1, corresponding to the ground vibrational state and the two l-doubled v=1 bending components. The pump–probe delay range recorded for the long-delay measurement is 1380–1412 ps, spanning alignment events around the 32 T_rev to 33 T_rev region. The plotted traces are normalized to the 32 3/4 T_rev revival of the ground-vibrational-level rotational constant B000. The measurement is configured to determine whether the centrifugal-distortion-precompensated response separates the ground-state and l-doubled bending-state contributions in time.

per_file.paper_title: Anderson Localization with Single Photons from a Quantum Emitter

expected_output.experiment_description: Fabrication procedure for the integrated photonic platform used to test whether single photons from a solid-state hBN emitter can undergo Anderson localization in a controlled off-diagonally disordered lattice. Two one-dimensional waveguide arrays are inscribed in a fused-silica chip, Corning 7980, by femtosecond direct laser writing. A Coherent Mira/RegA laser provides 800 nm, 150 fs pulses at 100 kHz, focused 200 µm below the sample surface using a 20× microscope objective with numerical aperture NA = 0.36. The substrate is translated relative to the focus with an Aerotech precision positioning system. The ordered control array is designed with 101 nominally identical waveguides separated by 21.9 µm, corresponding to nominal coupling κ0 = 0.08 mm^-1. The disordered array is designed with 101 nominally identical waveguides and inter-waveguide separations chosen so that nearest-neighbor couplings are independently sampled from a uniform distribution κ_n ~ U(κ0-Δ, κ0+Δ), with disorder strength Δ/κ0 = 0.8. The fabricated chip is intended to support end-facet imaging after propagation through the full waveguide length and to provide a periodic control and a coupling-disordered lattice for the Anderson-localization measurements.
