expected_output.experiment_description: Preparation and optical characterization of the room-temperature hexagonal-boron-nitride single-photon source used to inject nonclassical light into the disordered waveguide lattice. Two drops of solvent-exfoliated hBN solution, Boron Nitride Pristine Flakes in Solution from Graphene Supermarket, are drop-cast onto a marked silicon substrate. The substrate is annealed at 850 °C under a 1 Torr argon atmosphere in a tube furnace and then allowed to cool naturally to room temperature. A single defect is addressed in a custom confocal microscope using a 532 nm continuous-wave laser with 100 µW excitation power, focused by a Nikon 100× objective with NA = 0.9. The hBN sample position is controlled using a P-611.3 NanoCube three-axis piezo scanner with sub-10-nm resolution. Emission is collected through the same objective, separated from excitation using a 70:30 non-polarizing beamsplitter and pump-rejection filtering, and routed either to a spectrometer or to a fiber-based Hanbury Brown–Twiss interferometer. The zero-phonon-line region is isolated using a 20 nm-class bandpass filter centered on the selected emitter line. The second-order autocorrelation g^(2)(t) is normalized at long delay and fit with the three-level model g^(2)(t)=1-(1+a1)exp(-t/τ1)+a2 exp(-t/τ2), where τ1 is the antibunching recovery time associated with the excited-state lifetime under the measurement conditions, τ2 is a bunching timescale, and a1 and a2 are amplitudes. No detector-jitter correction is applied. The measurement is configured to establish the spectral emission line and whether emission is dominated by a single quantum defect for use in the Anderson-localization experiment.

single_photon_bandwidth_nm.description: The optical bandwidth of the hBN single-photon emission used for comparison with filtered laser excitation.

single_defect_single_photon_emission.description: Whether the autocorrelation measurement satisfies the single-emitter antibunching criterion for the addressed hBN defect.

expected_output.experiment_description: Ordered-array control measurement for the single-photon transport experiment. Single photons emitted by the characterized hBN defect at its selected zero-phonon line are isolated with a 20 nm bandpass filter, directed through free-space optics, and coupled into the central input waveguide of the 101-site periodic laser-written fused-silica waveguide array with 21.9 µm spacing and nominal coupling κ0 = 0.08 mm^-1. The waveguide chip output facet is imaged using an objective onto a single-photon-resolving electron-multiplying CCD camera. The spatial scope is the full visible end-facet span of the ordered array, approximately 0 to 1200 µm laterally in the plotted line scan; the two-dimensional EMCCD image is vertically binned to obtain a one-dimensional intensity profile across waveguide positions. This control is configured to determine the ordered-lattice transport behavior under the same single-photon source, coupling optics, chip imaging, and end-facet analysis used for the disordered Anderson-localization measurements.

ordered_array_single_photon_transport_re.description: The transport class assigned to the hBN single-photon end-facet intensity profile in the ordered periodic waveguide array.

expected_output.experiment_description: Bulk Anderson-localization measurement with hBN single photons in the coupling-disordered laser-written waveguide array. Single photons from the room-temperature hBN defect, spectrally filtered around the 619 nm zero-phonon-line region, are coupled by free-space optics into interior sites of the 101-waveguide disordered fused-silica array. The array uses off-diagonal disorder: nearest-neighbor couplings are designed to be uniformly distributed about κ0 with disorder strength Δ/κ0 = 0.8 while on-site propagation constants are nominally fixed. To avoid boundary reflections, the first bulk launch is placed at waveguide 30 of 101 and subsequent realizations are obtained by shifting the excitation site to neighboring waveguides. For each of 30 launch-site/disorder realizations, the output facet after propagation through the chip is imaged on a single-photon-resolving EMCCD. The end-facet intensity is analyzed over waveguide indices centered on the injection site, covering the localized central region and tails across approximately -20 to +20 relative waveguide indices. The peak intensity in each waveguide is extracted from the end-facet image, aligned to the injection site, averaged over the 30 realizations, and fit to I(n)=I0 exp(-2|n-n0|/ξ), where n is relative waveguide index, n0 is the launch index after alignment, I0 is a fitted amplitude, and ξ is the effective localization length in waveguide-site units. The measurement is designed to test whether the limited temporal coherence of a defect-based solid-state emitter is compatible with Anderson localization in an integrated photonic lattice.

experimental_bulk_localization_length_wa.description: The effective localization length extracted from the disorder-averaged hBN single-photon end-facet profile for bulk excitation.

experimental_bulk_localization_length_95.description: The 95% confidence interval half-width of the experimental bulk-excitation exponential-fit localization length.

expected_output.experiment_description: Boundary Anderson-localization measurement with hBN single photons in the same coupling-disordered laser-written waveguide array. Single photons from the room-temperature hBN defect, filtered around the 619 nm zero-phonon-line region, are coupled into the edge waveguide of the 101-site off-diagonally disordered fused-silica array. The output facet is imaged with the single-photon-resolving EMCCD through the same objective-based imaging system used for the bulk measurement. Four independent edge-excitation realizations are recorded and averaged. The spatial analysis covers the edge site and neighboring sites extending to approximately 30 waveguide indices into the array. Peak intensities are extracted per waveguide, averaged over the four realizations, and fit to I(n)=I0 exp(-2|n-n0|/ξ), where n is waveguide index measured inward from the boundary, n0 is the edge launch site, I0 is a fitted amplitude, and ξ is the effective localization length in waveguide-site units. This measurement probes how Anderson localization of hBN single photons is modified when the injection site has fewer neighboring scattering pathways at the lattice boundary.

experimental_edge_localization_length_wa.description: The effective localization length extracted from the averaged hBN single-photon end-facet profile for boundary excitation.

experimental_edge_localization_length_95.description: The 95% confidence interval half-width of the experimental edge-excitation exponential-fit localization length.

expected_output.experiment_description: Spectral-dependence control measurement testing whether the localization length in the coupling-disordered waveguide array changes across the wavelength range relevant to the hBN emitter. A filtered supercontinuum laser with bandwidth below 4 nm is coupled into interior sites of the same 101-waveguide off-diagonally disordered fused-silica array. The laser center wavelength is separately set to 607, 612, 617, 622, and 627 nm. For each wavelength, 30 bulk realizations are measured by exciting the central-region waveguide of a disordered lattice and shifting the launch site between neighboring waveguides, using the same end-facet EMCCD imaging, peak-per-waveguide extraction, disorder averaging, and exponential fitting procedure as in the hBN bulk single-photon experiment. The spatial scope is the relative waveguide-index region around the launch site used to capture the central peak and exponential tails. The measurement is configured to compare classical narrowband excitation with the finite-bandwidth hBN single-photon source under otherwise matched disordered-lattice conditions.

per_file.paper_title: Experimental demonstration of a coherent detector blinding attack on a real CV-QKD system

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: a controlled wideband incoherent optical-noise source is used to emulate the excess-noise signature that a collective eavesdropping attack would add to a continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) receiver, so that a later coherent detector-blinding stage can be tested against a known injected-noise baseline. The experiment uses only the Bob-side receiver of a polarization-diverse local-local-oscillator CV-QKD system. The receiver local oscillator is an Aerodiode 1550 nm DFB Model 5 laser driven by a Wavelength Electronics MPL250 laser driver and stabilized by a Wavelength Electronics PTC2.5K-CH temperature controller; its output passes through an optical isolator and an Agiltron LightBend 1x1 PM optical switch into a polarization-diverse receiver. The signal input passes through an Agiltron LightBend 1x1 optical switch and then a PBS that separates polarization components into two polarization-maintaining 50/50 beam splitters. The LO PBS is oriented with its fast axis shifted by 45 degrees relative to the LO polarization so that both receiver arms are illuminated. The two balanced detector channels are Wieserlabs WL-BPD1GA balanced optical receivers with 1.6 GHz bandwidth and DC cut-off below 300 kHz, digitized by a Texas Instruments ADC12DJ3200EVM at 3.2 GHz. The digital processing applied to each acquired horizontal and vertical polarization trace consists of downconversion around 400 MHz to baseband by multiplication with exp(-i 2 pi 400e6 t), root-raised-cosine filtering with roll-off factor 0.95 at 153.6 MBaud, polarization-drift recovery by combining the two polarization components assuming equal distribution between receiver arms, and variance computation. Thermal, shot, and noisy traces are acquired by controlling the receiver optical switches: both paths closed for Var[thermal], LO path open and signal path closed for Var[shot], and both paths open for Var[noisy]. Shot-noise units are defined as SNU = Var[shot] - Var[thermal]. The inferred noise variance is sigma_tilde_squared = Var[noisy]/SNU, the receiver thermal noise is epsilon_th = Var[thermal]/SNU, and the inferred excess noise is epsilon_tilde = (sigma_tilde_squared - 1 - epsilon_th)/(eta*T), using receiver efficiency eta = 0.90 and assumed channel transmission T = 0.5, corresponding to 15 km of standard single-mode fibre. The noise source consists of a Thorlabs EDFA100S erbium-doped fibre amplifier operated without input signal so that its amplified spontaneous emission supplies the incoherent optical noise; this output is attenuated by a Thorlabs V1550A voltage-controlled variable optical attenuator driven by a UNI-T UDP3305S power supply under PC serial control, and then combined through a WBC-2x2-13/15-10/90 90/10 beam splitter. The 90% splitter output is monitored by an OZ-Optics POM-300 optical power meter, with readings converted to the 10% port power using the known splitting ratio. The calibration/reproducibility measurement consists of four independent optical-power sweeps over the noise-source setting, varying the monitored noise power from -13.6 dBm to -51.25 dBm with smaller steps at higher attenuation. The spatial/geometric scope is the full two-arm polarization-diverse receiver input and both balanced-detector outputs after digital polarization recombination; reproducibility is assessed by comparing all four repeated sweeps over the same optical path and receiver processing chain. The measurement is configured to determine whether the ASE source provides a reproducible mapping from optical noise power to inferred CV-QKD excess noise in SNU.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: a coherent detector-blinding source is built to force an AC-coupled balanced detector in a real CV-QKD receiver into a nonlinear or clipped response regime. The attack concept uses a detuned optical field to exploit wavelength-dependent imbalance in the receiver optics and uses temporal modulation to pass through the balanced detector AC coupling, rather than relying on a constant optical blinding level. The tested receiver is the same polarization-diverse CV-QKD Bob receiver described in the paper: an Aerodiode 1550 nm DFB local oscillator, PBS splitting into two polarization-maintaining 50/50 beam splitters, two Wieserlabs WL-BPD1GA balanced optical receivers with 1.6 GHz bandwidth and low-frequency cut-off below 300 kHz, and a Texas Instruments ADC12DJ3200EVM digitizer sampling at 3.2 GHz with 12-bit precision. The blinding source consists of a Sumitomo Electric Industries SLV5410 laser diode emitting at 1344 nm. The diode current is supplied by a Rigol DG1032 function generator, enabling direct square-wave optical modulation at 10 MHz, and the diode temperature is controlled with a Thorlabs TED200C temperature controller. The modulated blinding field passes through a Thorlabs V1550A voltage-controlled variable optical attenuator driven by a UNI-T UDP3305S power supply under PC serial control. The attenuated light enters a Thorlabs TD1315R5F1 50/50 dual-window 1310/1550 nm beam splitter; one output is monitored by an OZ Optics POM-600 optical power meter and the other is combined with the signal fibre through a Thorlabs WD1350B wavelength-division multiplexer. A fibre polarization controller after the multiplexer is adjusted while monitoring both balanced-detector outputs so that the blinding-field amplitude delivered to the two polarization receiver arms is matched. For the standalone blinding-response measurement, the horizontal balanced-detector arm is monitored in the time domain while the blinding optical power is swept from -15 dBm to -13 dBm. The measurement scope is the horizontal polarization receiver arm and its ADC output over repeated cycles of the 10 MHz blinding modulation; the two-arm balance of the injected blinding field is checked by comparing the output amplitudes of both balanced receivers during polarization adjustment. The measurement is configured to identify the receiver stage that limits the response and to determine the blinding level at which the horizontal-channel digitized output reaches full-scale clipping.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: the complete coherent detector-blinding attack is tested on a real CV-QKD receiver by combining an ASE noise source, representing the excess-noise impact of a collective attack, with a modulated detuned blinding source that drives the receiver out of its normal linear operating regime. The apparatus is a reduced Bob-only implementation of the attack scenario: the exploitation stage is represented by the calibrated EDFA-based incoherent-noise source and the enabling stage is represented by the 1344 nm modulated blinding source. The receiver is the polarization-diverse local-local-oscillator CV-QKD receiver with Aerodiode 1550 nm DFB LO, Agiltron optical switches for thermal/shot/noisy acquisitions, PBS-based polarization splitting, two polarization-maintaining 50/50 beam splitters, two Wieserlabs WL-BPD1GA balanced optical receivers with 1.6 GHz bandwidth and 300 kHz low-frequency cut-off, and a Texas Instruments ADC12DJ3200EVM digitizer at 3.2 GHz. Digital processing consists of 400 MHz frequency recovery, root-raised-cosine filtering with roll-off 0.95 and 153.6 MBaud symbol rate, two-polarization combination for polarization-drift recovery, and variance computation. Shot-noise units are defined as SNU = Var[shot] - Var[thermal], with epsilon_tilde = (Var[noisy]/SNU - 1 - Var[thermal]/SNU)/(eta*T), eta = 0.90, and assumed channel transmission T = 0.5. The noise source is the Thorlabs EDFA100S ASE source attenuated by a Thorlabs V1550A VOA and injected through the 90/10 splitter path; the fixed corrected noise powers used in the attack measurement are -27.0 dBm, -28.3 dBm, -29.9 dBm, -30.8 dBm, and -31.8 dBm. The blinding source is the Sumitomo Electric Industries SLV5410 1344 nm diode directly square-wave modulated at 10 MHz by a Rigol DG1032, temperature controlled by a Thorlabs TED200C, attenuated by a Thorlabs V1550A VOA, monitored after a Thorlabs TD1315R5F1 50/50 beam splitter with an OZ Optics POM-600 optical power meter, and injected through a Thorlabs WD1350B wavelength-division multiplexer followed by a polarization controller adjusted to balance the blinding amplitudes in the receiver arms. The independent blinding-power sweep spans -15.64536 dBm to -12.53858 dBm for each fixed noise-source setting. The measurement scope is the complete two-balanced-detector polarization-diverse receiver after digital polarization recombination, with five independent fixed injected-noise conditions compared across the same blinding-power sweep. For evaluating whether a blinded receiver would accept a key, the receiver-estimated excess noise is compared with the positive-key-rate excess-noise threshold computed using the Denys-Brown-Leverrier arbitrary-modulation security proof for a probabilistically shaped 64-QAM constellation with Maxwell-Boltzmann-distributed constellation points at T = 0.5. per_file.paper_title: Pair-Breaking and Dimensionality in Spin-Orbit Coupled Superconductors

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: the zero-field superconducting transition of thickness-controlled LaBi2 thin films supplies the baseline critical temperature used to assess Pauli-limit violation and to compare KLB and Kharitonov-Feigel'man (KF) pair-breaking models. Measure rectangular Ge-capped LaBi2/MgO(001) films with approximate XRD-derived thicknesses t = 75, 34, 12, 8.5, 3.0, and 2.1 nm in a dilution refrigerator with base temperature about 20 mK. Use a linear four-point bond geometry on each rectangular film; drive an AC bias current of 100-500 nA at 10-20 Hz and read the longitudinal resistance with a lock-in amplifier. Sweep temperature through the superconducting transition at zero applied magnetic field. Normalize resistance by the normal-state resistance R0 measured above the transition, and define the experimental zero-field critical temperature T_c,H=0^Exp as the temperature where R/R0 = 0.5. The contacted transport path spans the macroscopic rectangular sample between voltage leads; the paper does not report the channel dimensions, contact spacing, lateral homogeneity map, or number of independent locations per thickness. The goal is to quantify how the intrinsic superconducting transition evolves as the film approaches the two-dimensional dirty-limit regime relevant to spin-orbit and magnetic pair-breaking.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: perpendicular-field superconducting transport supplies the superconducting coherence length used to assess whether LaBi2 films lie in the dirty limit, where the KLB and KF pair-breaking frameworks are applicable. Use the same Ge-capped LaBi2/MgO(001) rectangular films and four-point lock-in transport configuration as the zero-field transition experiment, in a dilution refrigerator with base temperature about 20 mK. Apply magnetic field perpendicular to the film plane and sweep temperature through the resistive transition for each thickness t = 75, 34, 12, 8.5, 3.0, and 2.1 nm. Determine H_c2^perp(T) from the same resistive transition criterion used for the main transport analysis. Fit H_c2^perp(T) to the single-gap Ginzburg-Landau relation H_c2^perp(T) = (Phi0/(2*pi*xi_ab^2)) * (1 - (T_c/T_c,H=0)^2), where Phi0 is the superconducting flux quantum, xi_ab is the in-plane superconducting coherence length, T_c is the transition temperature at applied perpendicular field, and T_c,H=0 is the zero-field transition temperature. The measurement samples the contacted rectangular transport path; the paper does not report channel dimensions, lateral mapping, or multiple-location statistics. The goal is to obtain the superconducting coherence length for comparison with mean free path estimates and to determine the dimensional/scattering regime relevant to pair-breaking.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: normal-state magnetotransport provides carrier-density, mobility, mean-free-path, Fermi-momentum, and transport-scattering estimates needed to evaluate the orbital pair-breaking term in the KF model for finite-thickness LaBi2. Measure normal-state sheet resistivity rho_xx and Hall resistivity rho_yx at T = 2 K for Ge-capped LaBi2/MgO(001) films, including representative thicknesses 75, 12, and 2.3 nm, under perpendicular magnetic field swept from 0 to 10 T. Use the same macroscopic rectangular four-point geometry; the paper does not report channel dimensions or lateral mapping. Fit rho_xx(B) and rho_yx(B) to the two-carrier Drude formulas rho_xx = (1/e)*[(p*mu_h+n*mu_e)+(p*mu_e+n*mu_h)*mu_h*mu_e*B^2]/[(p*mu_h+n*mu_e)^2+(p-n)^2*mu_h^2*mu_e^2*B^2] and rho_yx = (B/e)*[(p*mu_h^2-n*mu_e^2)+(p-n)^2*mu_h^2*mu_e^2*B^2]/[(p*mu_h+n*mu_e)^2+(p-n)^2*mu_h^2*mu_e^2*B^2], where e is elementary charge, B is perpendicular magnetic field, n and p are electron-like and hole-like carrier densities, and mu_e and mu_h are electron-like and hole-like mobilities. report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: the zero-field superconducting transition of thickness-controlled LaBi2 thin films supplies the baseline critical temperature used to assess Pauli-limit violation and to compare KLB and Kharitonov-Feigel'man (KF) pair-breaking models. Measure rectangular Ge-capped LaBi2/MgO(001) films with approximate XRD-derived thicknesses t = 75, 34, 12, 8.5, 3.0, and 2.1 nm in a dilution refrigerator with base temperature about 20 mK. Use a linear four-point bond geometry on each rectangular film; drive an AC bias current of 100-500 nA at 10-20 Hz and read the longitudinal resistance with a lock-in amplifier. Sweep temperature through the superconducting transition at zero applied magnetic field. Normalize resistance by the normal-state resistance R0 measured above the transition, and define the experimental zero-field critical temperature T_c,H=0^Exp as the temperature where R/R0 = 0.5. The contacted transport path spans the macroscopic rectangular sample between voltage leads; the paper does not report the channel dimensions, contact spacing, lateral homogeneity map, or number of independent locations per thickness. The goal is to quantify how the intrinsic superconducting transition evolves as the film approaches the two-dimensional dirty-limit regime relevant to spin-orbit and magnetic pair-breaking.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: perpendicular-field superconducting transport supplies the superconducting coherence length used to assess whether LaBi2 films lie in the dirty limit, where the KLB and KF pair-breaking frameworks are applicable. The goal is to obtain the superconducting coherence length for comparison with mean free path estimates and to determine the dimensional/scattering regime relevant to pair-breaking.

per_file.paper_title: Scalable Liquid-Crystal Integrated Silicon Nitride Photonic Circuits for Reconfigurable Quantum Interference

expected_output.experiment_description: The central device concept is a silicon-nitride Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) whose relative optical phase is tuned by reorienting a nematic liquid-crystal (LC) layer above a waveguide, targeting compact low-voltage reconfigurable quantum interference. For the electron-beam-defined devices used in the quantum measurements, fabricate the structure on a SiO2-on-Si wafer carrying a 300 nm LPCVD SiN layer. Define the LC-MZI waveguide pattern by electron-beam lithography using a JEOL JBX-8100FS, form 1 µm-wide fully etched SiN waveguides with 300 nm etch depth by reactive-ion etching, and deposit a 2 µm PECVD SiO2 upper cladding. Open a 3 µm-wide, 500 µm-long trench in the SiO2 cladding above the phase-shifter waveguide using 405 nm maskless lithography followed by reactive-ion etching. Deposit Cr/Au electrodes by e-beam evaporation and lift-off, pattern SU-8 microfluidic walls around the LC trench, dice a quartz lid to match the SU-8 structure, spin-coat and rub a polyimide alignment layer on the quartz to define the LC molecular orientation, align and bond the quartz lid to the SU-8 with UV-curable epoxy, and inject Merck E7 nematic liquid crystal into the sealed cavity by capillary action. Assess whether the target LC-integrated MZI structure is formed using an optical microscope image over the assembled circuit with a 2 mm scale reference, a cross-sectional SEM image of the LC trench/waveguide region before LC injection with a 1 µm scale reference, and crossed-polarized optical microscopy over the waveguide/electrode region with a 200 µm scale reference for rubbing directions parallel to and 45° relative to the polarizer. The goal is to determine whether the fabrication-and-assembly procedure produces the intended LC-filled, aligned SiN MZI phase-modulator geometry needed for voltage-controlled quantum interference, without using the downstream optical or quantum measurements as the criterion.

ebeam_lc_mzi_target_structure_formed.description: Whether the electron-beam-defined LC-integrated SiN MZI fabrication and assembly procedure produced the intended device structure under optical and SEM inspection.

lc_alignment_in_waveguide_region_detecte.description: Whether crossed-polarized optical microscopy detected LC alignment in the waveguide/electrode region of the assembled electron-beam-defined device.

expected_output.experiment_description: To test the operating mechanism of the LC phase shifter used for the reconfigurable SiN quantum-interference circuit, examine the LC-filled phase-modulator region by crossed-polarized optical microscopy while applying an AC square-wave voltage to the electrodes. Use the Merck E7 nematic liquid crystal in the trench above the SiN waveguide, with ordinary and extraordinary refractive indices specified for the design as no = 1.500 and ne = 1.685 at 1550 nm. Avoid DC driving; use an AC square wave in the approximately 500 Hz to 1 kHz range to reduce ionic-current screening. Configure the crossed polarizer/analyzer microscope so that the optical transmission through the LC region is sensitive to birefringence-induced polarization rotation. Compare the same phase-modulator region, imaged with a 30 µm scale reference near the waveguide and electrodes, at VLC = 0 V and at VLC = 3 V. The goal is to determine whether the electric field from the electrodes changes the LC molecular orientation in the waveguide-overlap region, which is the physical mechanism intended to tune the guided-mode effective index and hence the MZI phase.

field_induced_lc_reorientation_detected.description: Whether crossed-polarized optical microscopy detected voltage-induced LC reorientation in the phase-modulator region.

expected_output.experiment_description: Characterize the static electro-optic phase-shifting performance of the electron-beam-fabricated LC-MZI, which implements voltage-controlled phase tuning for quantum interference by changing the LC-clad SiN waveguide effective index. Use MZIs composed of two 2×2 multimode-interference couplers and an LC phase-modulator section inside SU-8 walls. The SiN waveguide cross section is 300 nm high and 1 µm wide, the SiO2 upper cladding is 2 µm thick outside the LC trench, and the LC interaction trench over the waveguide is 3 µm wide and 500 µm long. Apply an AC square-wave voltage to the LC electrodes in the approximately 500 Hz to 1 kHz range. For the unbalanced MZI, measure the S42 optical transmission spectrum by sweeping wavelength from 1500 nm to 1600 nm at VLC = 0 V and at a voltage selected to shift the interferometric fringe by a half period. For the balanced MZI with the same 500 µm modulator length, measure the S32 optical transmission spectrum over 1540 nm to 1580 nm at five applied voltages spanning 0 V to the switching-voltage range. Define Vpi as the voltage required to produce a π optical phase shift in the LC phase shifter, and define Vpi·L as Vpi multiplied by the LC modulator length L expressed in millimetres. Determine the extinction ratio of the balanced MZI from the maximum-to-minimum transmission contrast in the voltage-tuned spectral response. The measurement targets CMOS-compatible, low-voltage phase modulation in the LC-integrated SiN MZI, not thermal phase tuning.

balanced_mzi_vpi_V.description: The measured voltage required for a π phase shift in the 500 µm LC phase shifter of the balanced electron-beam-fabricated MZI.

balanced_mzi_extinction_ratio_dB.description: The measured optical extinction ratio between maximum and minimum transmissions of the voltage-tuned balanced LC-MZI.

expected_output.experiment_description: Measure the temporal switching response of the electron-beam-fabricated LC-MZI phase modulator to determine whether the LC-based SiN platform is suitable for circuit reconfiguration and active phase stabilization in quantum photonic circuits. Use the unbalanced LC-MZI consisting of two 2×2 multimode-interference couplers and a 500 µm-long LC phase-modulator trench over a 300 nm-high, 1 µm-wide SiN waveguide. Drive the LC electrodes with a 1 kHz AC square-wave voltage whose amplitude is set to the Vpi condition obtained from the static wavelength-sweep calibration. Monitor the S32 optical output at a fixed wavelength of 1549.2 nm, selected from the unpowered interferometer spectrum for high sensitivity to phase changes. Record the time-dependent optical power during the electrical transition and define the rise time and fall time from the optical transition in the time trace using the convention applied in the plotted transient measurement. The spatial scope is the same LC interaction region used for the static phase-modulation characterization, bounded by the SU-8 LC cell and electrodes.

lc_mzi_rise_time_ms.description: The measured optical rise time of the LC-MZI output in response to the 1 kHz Vpi square-wave drive.

lc_mzi_fall_time_ms.description: The measured optical fall time of the LC-MZI output in response to the 1 kHz Vpi square-wave drive.

expected_output.experiment_description: Before using the integrated LC-MZI for on-chip quantum interference, benchmark the indistinguishability of the photon-pair source with a fiber beam splitter. Generate photon pairs by spontaneous parametric down-conversion in a 7 mm-long type-II periodically poled potassium titanyl phosphate crystal pumped by a 780 nm continuous-wave tunable diode laser (Toptica TA Pro). Separate the pair with a polarizing beam splitter, reject residual pump light using long-pass filters, and independently prepare the polarization in each arm using a half-wave plate and a quarter-wave plate. Use a translation stage in one path to sweep the relative arrival delay through the Hong-Ou-Mandel interference region. Couple the photons through fiber optics to a fiber beam splitter and detect the outputs with superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. Record photon arrival times with a quTAG time-to-digital converter for time-correlated single-photon counting. Compute the accidental-corrected Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility as V = (Cmax - Cmin)/(Cmax + Cmin), where Cmax is the coincidence rate away from temporal overlap and Cmin is the coincidence rate at the interference minimum after accidental-coincidence correction. This control experiment targets the source quality required for later voltage-controlled two-photon interference in the LC-integrated SiN circuit.

fiber_hom_visibility_percent.description: The accidental-corrected Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility measured for the photon-pair source using a fiber beam splitter.

expected_output.experiment_description: Test voltage-controlled on-chip two-photon interference in the electron-beam-fabricated LC-MZI, the central demonstration that LC phase tuning in a SiN circuit preserves quantum coherence while reconfiguring the two-photon output state. Generate photon pairs in a 7 mm-long type-II PPKTP crystal pumped by a 780 nm continuous-wave tunable diode laser, separate them with a polarizing beam splitter, reject pump light with long-pass filters, set polarization with half-wave and quarter-wave plates, and use a translation stage to control the relative delay. Couple the two photons into the two input ports of the LC-MZI with lensed fibers and collect both output ports with lensed fibers. Use polarization controllers to optimize collection, superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors for detection, and a quTAG time-to-digital converter for time-correlated coincidence counting. The on-chip device contains two 2×2 multimode-interference couplers and a 500 µm-long LC phase shifter in one MZI arm; the LC is driven by an AC square-wave voltage in the approximately 500 Hz to 1 kHz range. First set the relative delay to zero path difference, τ = 0, so that the photons arrive simultaneously at the interferometer, and sweep the LC voltage over the plotted modulation range to compare the voltage dependence of two-photon coincidences with the single-photon cross-port transmission. Then perform full delay-line sweeps at fixed LC voltages including 1.06 V, 1.22 V, and 1.40 V. Define the two-photon interference visibility using the same normalized coincidence-contrast convention V = (Cmax - Cmin)/(Cmax + Cmin), with Cmax and Cmin taken from the fitted delay-dependent coincidence curve at each fixed voltage. The measurement scope is the integrated MZI active region between input ports 1 and 2 and output ports 3 and 4, with the two-photon interaction occurring at the on-chip interferometer while phase is tuned by the LC layer.

two_photon_coincidence_voltage_oscillati.description: The measured oscillation frequency of the zero-delay two-photon coincidence signal as a multiple of the single-photon transmission oscillation frequency under the LC voltage sweep.

on_chip_two_photon_visibility_at_1p06V_p.description: The fitted two-photon interference visibility measured from the on-chip delay sweep at fixed LC voltage of 1.06 V.

on_chip_two_photon_visibility_at_1p22V_p.description: The fitted two-photon interference visibility measured from the on-chip delay sweep at fixed LC voltage of 1.22 V.

expected_output.experiment_description: Demonstrate scalability of the LC-integrated SiN photonic-circuit concept by replacing electron-beam waveguide patterning with wafer-scale i-line stepper lithography and by using a device architecture that physically separates the LC trench from the electrodes. Start from a SiO2-on-Si wafer with an LPCVD SiN layer and pattern LC-MZI waveguides on a 4-inch wafer using a Nikon NSR-2005i10C i-line stepper. Form the SiN waveguides by reactive-ion etching, deposit the PECVD SiO2 upper cladding, open the LC trench above the waveguide using 405 nm maskless lithography and reactive-ion etching, deposit Cr/Au electrodes by e-beam evaporation and lift-off with a layout in which the electrodes are not in direct contact with the LC trench region, and pattern SU-8 microfluidic walls. Dice devices, prepare a rubbed-polyimide-coated quartz lid, bond it to the SU-8 structure using UV-curable epoxy, and inject Merck E7 LC by capillary action. Inspect the wafer-scale patterning over the 4-inch wafer before LC injection using an image with a 1 inch scale reference, inspect a diced/bonded/injected chip using an image with a 1 cm scale reference, and inspect the LC trench/electrode/waveguide cross section by SEM using a 2 µm scale reference. The goal is to determine whether the scalable process forms the target LC-MZI structures with electrode-LC separation appropriate for robust large-scale production, independently of any electro-optic tuning result.

stepper_device_electrode_lc_physical_iso.description: Whether SEM inspection of the stepper-fabricated architecture confirmed physical separation between the LC trench region and the electrodes.

expected_output.experiment_description: Quantify the electro-optic phase-shifting performance of the stepper-lithography LC-MZI platform, which is intended to scale the low-voltage LC-integrated SiN reconfigurable quantum-photonic architecture beyond individual electron-beam-written devices. Use unbalanced MZIs fabricated on the 4-inch wafer by i-line stepper lithography, with LC phase-modulator lengths L = 500 µm, 1000 µm, and 2000 µm and electrode gaps g = 5 µm, 6 µm, and 7 µm. The process uses SiN waveguides on SiO2/Si, PECVD SiO2 cladding, opened LC trenches, Cr/Au electrodes physically isolated from the LC region, SU-8 walls, a rubbed-polyimide quartz lid, and capillary-injected Merck E7 LC. For spectral tuning, measure the unbalanced-MZI transmission by sweeping wavelength from 1500 nm to 1600 nm, including a representative device with L = 2000 µm and g = 5 µm at 0 V and at the π-phase-shift voltage. For voltage tuning, measure normalized transmission versus applied voltage at 1557 nm. Extract Vpi, defined as the voltage required for a π optical phase shift, for each electrode-gap and modulator-length combination from the voltage-dependent transmission or the spectral fringe shift. The spatial scope is the LC trench/electrode region of each MZI geometry on the stepper-fabricated wafer-scale platform; comparisons are made across the nine specified L and g design combinations.

report_experiments.experiment_description: The central device concept is a silicon-nitride Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) whose relative optical phase is tuned by reorienting a nematic liquid-crystal (LC) layer above a waveguide, targeting compact low-voltage reconfigurable quantum interference. For the electron-beam-defined devices used in the quantum measurements, fabricate the structure on a SiO2-on-Si wafer carrying a 300 nm LPCVD SiN layer. Define the LC-MZI waveguide pattern by electron-beam lithography using a JEOL JBX-8100FS, form 1 µm-wide fully etched SiN waveguides with 300 nm etch depth by reactive-ion etching, and deposit a 2 µm PECVD SiO2 upper cladding. Open a 3 µm-wide, 500 µm-long trench in the SiO2 cladding above the phase-shifter waveguide using 405 nm maskless lithography followed by reactive-ion etching. Deposit Cr/Au electrodes by e-beam evaporation and lift-off, pattern SU-8 microfluidic walls around the LC trench, dice a quartz lid to match the SU-8 structure, spin-coat and rub a polyimide alignment layer on the quartz to define the LC molecular orientation, align and bond the quartz lid to the SU-8 with UV-curable epoxy, and inject Merck E7 nematic liquid crystal into the sealed cavity by capillary action. Assess whether the target LC-integrated MZI structure is formed using an optical microscope image over the assembled circuit with a 2 mm scale reference, a cross-sectional SEM image of the LC trench/waveguide region before LC injection with a 1 µm scale reference, and crossed-polarized optical microscopy over the waveguide/electrode region with a 200 µm scale reference for rubbing directions parallel to and 45° relative to the polarizer. The goal is to determine whether the fabrication-and-assembly procedure produces the intended LC-filled, aligned SiN MZI phase-modulator geometry needed for voltage-controlled quantum interference, without using the downstream optical or quantum measurements as the criterion.

result_rows.description: Whether the electron-beam-defined LC-integrated SiN MZI fabrication and assembly procedure produced the intended device structure under optical and SEM inspection.
Whether crossed-polarized optical microscopy detected LC alignment in the waveguide/electrode region of the assembled electron-beam-defined device.

report_experiments.experiment_description: To test the operating mechanism of the LC phase shifter used for the reconfigurable SiN quantum-interference circuit, examine the LC-filled phase-modulator region by crossed-polarized optical microscopy while applying an AC square-wave voltage to the electrodes. Use the Merck E7 nematic liquid crystal in the trench above the SiN waveguide, with ordinary and extraordinary refractive indices specified for the design as no = 1.500 and ne = 1.685 at 1550 nm. Avoid DC driving; use an AC square wave in the approximately 500 Hz to 1 kHz range to reduce ionic-current screening. Configure the crossed polarizer/analyzer microscope so that the optical transmission through the LC region is sensitive to birefringence-induced polarization rotation. Compare the same phase-modulator region, imaged with a 30 µm scale reference near the waveguide and electrodes, at VLC = 0 V and at VLC = 3 V. The goal is to determine whether the electric field from the electrodes changes the LC molecular orientation in the waveguide-overlap region, which is the physical mechanism intended to tune the guided-mode effective index and hence the MZI phase.

result_rows.description: Whether crossed-polarized optical microscopy detected voltage-induced LC reorientation in the phase-modulator region.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Characterize the static electro-optic phase-shifting performance of the electron-beam-fabricated LC-MZI, which implements voltage-controlled phase tuning for quantum interference by changing the LC-clad SiN waveguide effective index. Use MZIs composed of two 2×2 multimode-interference couplers and an LC phase-modulator section inside SU-8 walls. The SiN waveguide cross section is 300 nm high and 1 µm wide, the SiO2 upper cladding is 2 µm thick outside the LC trench, and the LC interaction trench over the waveguide is 3 µm wide and 500 µm long. Apply an AC square-wave voltage to the LC electrodes in the approximately 500 Hz to 1 kHz range. For the unbalanced MZI, measure the S42 optical transmission spectrum by sweeping wavelength from 1500 nm to 1600 nm at VLC = 0 V and at a voltage selected to shift the interferometric fringe by a half period. For the balanced MZI with the same 500 µm modulator length, measure the S32 optical transmission spectrum over 1540 nm to 1580 nm at five applied voltages spanning 0 V to the switching-voltage range. Define Vpi as the voltage required to produce a π optical phase shift in the LC phase shifter, and define Vpi·L as Vpi multiplied by the LC modulator length L expressed in millimetres. Determine the extinction ratio of the balanced MZI from the maximum-to-minimum transmission contrast in the voltage-tuned spectral response. The measurement targets CMOS-compatible, low-voltage phase modulation in the LC-integrated SiN MZI, not thermal phase tuning.

result_rows.description: The measured voltage required for a π phase shift in the 500 µm LC phase shifter of the unbalanced electron-beam-fabricated MZI.
The measured Vpi·L modulation-efficiency product for the 500 µm LC phase shifter in the unbalanced electron-beam-fabricated MZI.
The measured voltage required for a π phase shift in the 500 µm LC phase shifter of the balanced electron-beam-fabricated MZI.
The measured optical extinction ratio between maximum and minimum transmissions of the voltage-tuned balanced LC-MZI.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Measure the temporal switching response of the electron-beam-fabricated LC-MZI phase modulator to determine whether the LC-based SiN platform is suitable for circuit reconfiguration and active phase stabilization in quantum photonic circuits. Use the unbalanced LC-MZI consisting of two 2×2 multimode-interference couplers and a 500 µm-long LC phase-modulator trench over a 300 nm-high, 1 µm-wide SiN waveguide. Drive the LC electrodes with a 1 kHz AC square-wave voltage whose amplitude is set to the Vpi condition obtained from the static wavelength-sweep calibration. Monitor the S32 optical output at a fixed wavelength of 1549.2 nm, selected from the unpowered interferometer spectrum for high sensitivity to phase changes. Record the time-dependent optical power during the electrical transition and define the rise time and fall time from the optical transition in the time trace using the convention applied in the plotted transient measurement. The spatial scope is the same LC interaction region used for the static phase-modulation characterization, bounded by the SU-8 LC cell and electrodes.

result_rows.description: The measured optical rise time of the LC-MZI output in response to the 1 kHz Vpi square-wave drive.
The measured optical fall time of the LC-MZI output in response to the 1 kHz Vpi square-wave drive.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Before using the integrated LC-MZI for on-chip quantum interference, benchmark the indistinguishability of the photon-pair source with a fiber beam splitter. Generate photon pairs by spontaneous parametric down-conversion in a 7 mm-long type-II periodically poled potassium titanyl phosphate crystal pumped by a 780 nm continuous-wave tunable diode laser (Toptica TA Pro). Separate the pair with a polarizing beam splitter, reject residual pump light using long-pass filters, and independently prepare the polarization in each arm using a half-wave plate and a quarter-wave plate. Use a translation stage in one path to sweep the relative arrival delay through the Hong-Ou-Mandel interference region. Couple the photons through fiber optics to a fiber beam splitter and detect the outputs with superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. Record photon arrival times with a quTAG time-to-digital converter for time-correlated single-photon counting. Compute the accidental-corrected Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility as V = (Cmax - Cmin)/(Cmax + Cmin), where Cmax is the coincidence rate away from temporal overlap and Cmin is the coincidence rate at the interference minimum after accidental-coincidence correction. This control experiment targets the source quality required for later voltage-controlled two-photon interference in the LC-integrated SiN circuit.

result_rows.description: The accidental-corrected Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility measured for the photon-pair source using a fiber beam splitter.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Test voltage-controlled on-chip two-photon interference in the electron-beam-fabricated LC-MZI, the central demonstration that LC phase tuning in a SiN circuit preserves quantum coherence while reconfiguring the two-photon output state. Generate photon pairs in a 7 mm-long type-II PPKTP crystal pumped by a 780 nm continuous-wave tunable diode laser, separate them with a polarizing beam splitter, reject pump light with long-pass filters, set polarization with half-wave and quarter-wave plates, and use a translation stage to control the relative delay. Couple the two photons into the two input ports of the LC-MZI with lensed fibers and collect both output ports with lensed fibers. Use polarization controllers to optimize collection, superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors for detection, and a quTAG time-to-digital converter for time-correlated coincidence counting. The on-chip device contains two 2×2 multimode-interference couplers and a 500 µm-long LC phase shifter in one MZI arm; the LC is driven by an AC square-wave voltage in the approximately 500 Hz to 1 kHz range. First set the relative delay to zero path difference, τ = 0, so that the photons arrive simultaneously at the interferometer, and sweep the LC voltage over the plotted modulation range to compare the voltage dependence of two-photon coincidences with the single-photon cross-port transmission. Then perform full delay-line sweeps at fixed LC voltages including 1.06 V, 1.22 V, and 1.40 V. Define the two-photon interference visibility using the same normalized coincidence-contrast convention V = (Cmax - Cmin)/(Cmax + Cmin), with Cmax and Cmin taken from the fitted delay-dependent coincidence curve at each fixed voltage. The measurement scope is the integrated MZI active region between input ports 1 and 2 and output ports 3 and 4, with the two-photon interaction occurring at the on-chip interferometer while phase is tuned by the LC layer.

The fitted two-photon interference visibility measured from the on-chip delay sweep at fixed LC voltage of 1.06 V.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Demonstrate scalability of the LC-integrated SiN photonic-circuit concept by replacing electron-beam waveguide patterning with wafer-scale i-line stepper lithography and by using a device architecture that physically separates the LC trench from the electrodes. Start from a SiO2-on-Si wafer with an LPCVD SiN layer and pattern LC-MZI waveguides on a 4-inch wafer using a Nikon NSR-2005i10C i-line stepper. Form the SiN waveguides by reactive-ion etching, deposit the PECVD SiO2 upper cladding, open the LC trench above the waveguide using 405 nm maskless lithography and reactive-ion etching, deposit Cr/Au electrodes by e-beam evaporation and lift-off with a layout in which the electrodes are not in direct contact with the LC trench region, and pattern SU-8 microfluidic walls. Dice devices, prepare a rubbed-polyimide-coated quartz lid, bond it to the SU-8 structure using UV-curable epoxy, and inject Merck E7 LC by capillary action. Inspect the wafer-scale patterning over the 4-inch wafer before LC injection using an image with a 1 inch scale reference, inspect a diced/bonded/injected chip using an image with a 1 cm scale reference, and inspect the LC trench/electrode/waveguide cross section by SEM using a 2 µm scale reference. The goal is to determine whether the scalable process forms the target LC-MZI structures with electrode-LC separation appropriate for robust large-scale production, independently of any electro-optic tuning result.

result_rows.description: Whether the stepper-lithography wafer-scale process produced LC-MZI structures across a 4-inch wafer under wafer-level and chip-level inspection.
Whether SEM inspection of the stepper-fabricated architecture confirmed physical separation between the LC trench region and the electrodes.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Quantify the electro-optic phase-shifting performance of the stepper-lithography LC-MZI platform, which is intended to scale the low-voltage LC-integrated SiN reconfigurable quantum-photonic architecture beyond individual electron-beam-written devices. Use unbalanced MZIs fabricated on the 4-inch wafer by i-line stepper lithography, with LC phase-modulator lengths L = 500 µm, 1000 µm, and 2000 µm and electrode gaps g = 5 µm, 6 µm, and 7 µm. The process uses SiN waveguides on SiO2/Si, PECVD SiO2 cladding, opened LC trenches, Cr/Au electrodes physically isolated from the LC region, SU-8 walls, a rubbed-polyimide quartz lid, and capillary-injected Merck E7 LC. For spectral tuning, measure the unbalanced-MZI transmission by sweeping wavelength from 1500 nm to 1600 nm, including a representative device with L = 2000 µm and g = 5 µm at 0 V and at the π-phase-shift voltage. For voltage tuning, measure normalized transmission versus applied voltage at 1557 nm. Extract Vpi, defined as the voltage required for a π optical phase shift, for each electrode-gap and modulator-length combination from the voltage-dependent transmission or the spectral fringe shift. The spatial scope is the LC trench/electrode region of each MZI geometry on the stepper-fabricated wafer-scale platform; comparisons are made across the nine specified L and g design combinations.

per_file.paper_title: Realization of Backward Retrieval in a Stark-modulated Spin-wave Quantum Memory

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: implement a Stark-echo-modulated spin-wave quantum memory in Eu3+:Y2SiO5, using electric-field-induced opposite Stark phases in inversion-related Eu3+ sub-ensembles to suppress unwanted coherent echo emission without removing absorbers, thereby preserving the full optical depth for forward or backward retrieval. The preparation procedure is performed on a 0.1% Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystal with dimensions 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm along the D1, D2, and C2 axes, using Eu3+ ions at site 1. The crystal is cooled to 1.8 K in a cryostat. Optical fields propagate along the C2 axis and are polarized along D1. Copper electrodes attached to the crystal with silver paint provide electric fields parallel to D1. A collinear counter-propagating optical arrangement is aligned with a fiber coupler; optical pulses are generated and modulated with two acousto-optic modulators, and avalanche-photodiode detection is gated with a separate acousto-optic modulator. The ensemble-preparation recipe consists of repeated class cleaning and spin-polarization pulse sequences: 1-ms frequency-chirped optical pulses with 100 µW peak power are applied, with the class-cleaning block repeated 200 times and the spin-polarization blocks repeated 200 times as indicated for the addressed Eu3+ hyperfine transitions. The spatial scope is the optical mode passing through the full 10-mm crystal length along C2, targeting the ensemble absorption feature used as the active memory region rather than isolated microscopic sites. The goal is to determine whether this preparation creates a spectrally isolated absorption feature suitable for the Stark-echo memory protocol, quantified by optical depth and spectral bandwidth from the transmission spectrum.

prepared_absorption_feature_optical_dept.description: The optical depth of the prepared Eu3+ absorption feature used as the active memory transition.

prepared_absorption_feature_bandwidth_MH.description: The spectral bandwidth of the prepared Eu3+ absorption feature used for memory operation.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: characterize the Stark control mechanism required for a Stark-echo-modulated spin-wave quantum memory in Eu3+:Y2SiO5, where inversion-related Eu3+ sub-ensembles acquire opposite Stark phases so that a first electric-field pulse can scramble collective emission and a second electric-field pulse can rephase it. The measurement uses the same 0.1% Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystal, 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm along D1, D2, and C2, cooled to 1.8 K, with optical fields propagating along C2 and polarized along D1. Electric fields are applied parallel to D1 using copper electrodes attached with silver paint. The spectrally prepared ensemble from class cleaning and spin polarization is probed over the optical beam path through the full crystal length. Stark modulation is measured with two-pulse photon-echo, four-level photon-echo, and Stark-echo sequences. In the Stark-echo verification, one Stark pulse at time t1 is fixed and the second Stark-pulse area at time t7 is swept; the memory operating point uses a Stark-pulse area of 9.25 V cm^-1 µs. The Stark shift convention is Δν = −L Δµ·E, where Δν is the optical-frequency shift, L is the local-field correction factor, Δµ is the difference in permanent electric dipole moments between the two levels, and E is the applied electric field. For a Stark pulse of duration τS and electric field ES, the two inversion-related sub-ensembles accumulate relative phase 2φS = 2(Δµ·ES/ℏ)τS. The goal is to calibrate the linear Stark coefficient that determines the phase scrambling and rephasing used in the memory sequence.

linear_stark_coefficient_kHz_per_V_cm_mi.description: The measured optical-frequency Stark shift coefficient for the addressed Eu3+:Y2SiO5 transition under an electric field along D1.

linear_stark_coefficient_uncertainty_kHz.description: The one-standard-deviation uncertainty of the measured linear Stark coefficient.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: test forward retrieval in the Stark-echo spin-wave quantum memory, in which four optical π pulses and two Stark pulses are used to suppress the ordinary four-level echo and retrieve a Stark echo while preserving the full prepared optical depth of the Eu3+:Y2SiO5 ensemble. The active medium is a 0.1% Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystal, 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm along D1, D2, and C2, cooled to 1.8 K. Eu3+ site-1 hyperfine levels form the four-level scheme. Optical pulses propagate along C2 with polarization along D1. The electric field is applied along D1 through copper electrodes attached with silver paint. The prepared absorption feature has its optical mode extending through the 10-mm crystal length along C2. The forward-retrieval sequence uses an input signal at t0 followed by a first Stark pulse at t1, optical π pulses at t2 and t3 to transfer optical coherence to the ground-state spin coherence |±1/2>g ↔ |±3/2>g, optical π pulses at t5 and t6 to transfer through the excited-state spin coherence |±3/2>e ↔ |±5/2>e, and a second Stark pulse at t7. The Stark pulse area used for memory operation is 9.25 V cm^-1 µs. The forward phase-matching condition is k_echo = k0 − k2 − k3 + k5 + k6, where ki is the wave vector of the optical pulse at time ti; the echo time is t8 = t0 − t2 − t3 + t5 + t6. Direct avalanche-photodiode detection is used for the retrieved Stark-echo intensity, with the detection window gated by an acousto-optic modulator. The timing of the π pulses is adjusted to temporally separate the Stark echo from four-level-echo background; the reported memory-efficiency point is evaluated at a storage/retrieval time of 29 µs. Coherence dynamics are measured by heterodyne detection of Stark-echo decay curves while independently varying the intervals t6−t3 and t5−t2 over the plotted range from about 20 µs to 60 µs. The data are fitted with ηSE = ηretrieval ηpm ηcontrol^4 ηdecay, where ηSE is total memory efficiency, ηretrieval is the optical-depth-dependent retrieval factor, ηpm is phase-matching efficiency, ηcontrol is the population-transfer efficiency of each π pulse, and ηdecay is the decoherence term. For forward retrieval ηretrieval = d^2 exp(−d), with d = αL the optical depth. The decoherence model is ηdecay = exp[−Γ13^2(t5−t2)^2/(2 ln2/π^2)] exp[−Γ35^2(t6−t3)^2/(2 ln2/π^2) − 2γ(t6−t3)], where Γ13 is the inhomogeneous linewidth of |±1/2>g ↔ |±3/2>g, Γ35 is the inhomogeneous linewidth of |±3/2>e ↔ |±5/2>e, and γ is the effective optical decoherence rate. For the co-propagating forward geometry, ηpm is taken as unity when extracting ηcontrol.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: test backward retrieval in the Stark-echo spin-wave quantum memory, using Stark phase scrambling and rephasing to enable a retrieval direction that avoids the reabsorption-limited forward-emission geometry while retaining the full prepared optical depth of the Eu3+:Y2SiO5 ensemble. The active medium is a 0.1% Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystal, 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm along D1, D2, and C2, cooled to 1.8 K. Optical fields address Eu3+ site-1 hyperfine transitions, propagate along the C2 axis in a collinear counter-propagating geometry, and are polarized along D1. Electric fields are applied along D1 using copper electrodes attached with silver paint. The optical mode passes through the 10-mm crystal length and defines the active memory region. The backward-retrieval pulse sequence contains the same Stark-echo elements as the forward protocol: input signal at t0, first Stark pulse at t1, two optical π pulses at t2 and t3, two later optical π pulses at t5 and t6, and a second Stark pulse at t7, with the memory Stark-pulse area set to 9.25 V cm^-1 µs. To target backward phase matching, the propagation direction of the π pulse at t5 is reversed, the two π pulses at t5 and t6 are interchanged relative to the forward sequence, and the timing is adjusted to separate background four-level echoes from the Stark echo by spatial and temporal discrimination. The phase-matching convention is k_echo = k0 − k2 − k3 + k5 + k6, where ki is the optical wave vector at ti; the echo time is t8 = t0 − t2 − t3 + t5 + t6. Direct avalanche-photodiode detection measures the retrieved Stark-echo intensity, and heterodyne detection records Stark-echo decay profiles while varying t6−t3 and t5−t2 over the plotted range from about 25 µs to 60 µs. The reported memory-efficiency point is evaluated at 23 µs. Decay data are fitted with ηSE = ηretrieval ηpm ηcontrol^4 ηdecay, with backward retrieval factor ηretrieval = [1 − exp(−d)]^2, d = αL, and ηdecay = exp[−Γ13^2(t5−t2)^2/(2 ln2/π^2)] exp[−Γ35^2(t6−t3)^2/(2 ln2/π^2) − 2γ(t6−t3)], where Γ13 and Γ35 are the ground- and excited-state spin-transition inhomogeneous linewidths and γ is the effective optical decoherence rate.

backward_combined_phase_matching_and_con.description: The extracted combined factor ηpm ηcontrol^4 for the backward geometry, where ηpm is phase-matching efficiency and ηcontrol is the population-transfer efficiency per π pulse.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: quantify coherent-noise pathways in the Stark-echo memory and test whether Stark phase control suppresses unwanted photon-echo and free-induction components that would otherwise contaminate quantum storage. The experiment uses the same prepared 0.1% Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystal ensemble at 1.8 K, with optical propagation along C2, polarization along D1, and electric-field pulses along D1. The memory sequence is run without an input signal so that any detected free-induction decay or two-pulse-echo noise originates from the applied optical π pulses. The control pulses address the relevant ωb and ωd transitions in the four-level Eu3+ hyperfine scheme. Detection is performed with a gated avalanche photodiode over the output time window following the final π pulse and around the expected two-pulse echo. Measurements are compared for the same optical pulse sequence with and without the Stark electric-field pulse at t7. The spatial scope is the full optical mode through the prepared ensemble; no position-resolved imaging is involved. The intended metric is the residual coherent noise fraction relative to the corresponding no-Stark-field pulse sequence.

fid_noise_residual_fraction_upper_bound_.description: The upper bound on the free-induction-decay noise intensity remaining after applying the Stark pulse, normalized to the corresponding free-induction-decay noise intensity without the Stark pulse.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: use measured four-level-echo noise in the Stark-echo memory to infer control-pulse transfer efficiency and the backward phase-matching limitation. The same 0.1% Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystal ensemble is prepared by class cleaning and spin polarization, cooled to 1.8 K, and driven with optical pulses along the C2 axis with D1 polarization; electric fields are applied along D1. In the forward and backward Stark-echo memory geometries, an input signal at t0 and four π pulses at t2, t3, t5, and t6 can generate parasitic four-level echoes 4LE0mn when the input excitation combines with π pulses at tm and tn. The four-level-echo wave-vector condition is k4LE = −k0 + kπ1 + kπ2, where k0 is the input-signal wave vector and kπ1 and kπ2 are the wave vectors of the two π pulses forming the parasitic echo. In the forward sequence, the detectable parasitic echoes include 4LE026, 4LE035, and 4LE056; in the backward sequence, the geometry produces two backward-propagating four-level echoes and one forward-propagating four-level echo. Avalanche-photodiode detection records the Stark echo and the temporally separated four-level-echo backgrounds, with the timing set so that the Stark echo and parasitic echoes occupy distinct detection windows. The inference uses the intensity scalings ISE ∝ ηcontrol^4 and I4LE ∝ (1−ηcontrol)^2 ηcontrol^2, where ISE is Stark-echo intensity, I4LE is four-level-echo noise intensity, and ηcontrol is the transfer efficiency of each π pulse; the relevant decoherence factors are included. For the backward sequence, the inferred ηcontrol is combined with the measured backward efficiency and decay model to estimate ηpm, the spatial phase-matching efficiency of the counter-propagating geometry.

forward_control_pulse_efficiency_percent.description: The π-pulse population-transfer efficiency inferred from the measured forward Stark-echo to four-level-echo intensity ratio and decoherence corrections.

backward_control_pulse_efficiency_percen.description: The π-pulse population-transfer efficiency inferred from the measured backward Stark-echo to four-level-echo intensity ratio and decoherence corrections.

backward_phase_matching_efficiency_perce.description: The phase-matching efficiency inferred for the backward-retrieval geometry after using the noise-ratio-derived control-pulse efficiency in the memory-efficiency model.

expected_output.experiment_description: Central concept: evaluate whether the Stark-echo spin-wave memory preserves time-bin photonic qubits with high conditional fidelity for both forward and backward retrieval while suppressing coherent noise through Stark modulation. The memory uses the same 0.1% Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystal at 1.8 K, Eu3+ site-1 hyperfine transitions, optical propagation along C2 with D1 polarization, and electric-field pulses along D1. The input qubit is |ψ> = (|e> + exp(iΔα)|l>)/sqrt(2), where |e> and |l> are the early and late temporal modes and Δα is their relative phase. Forward-retrieval qubit measurements use a time-bin separation Δt = 4 µs; backward-retrieval qubit measurements use Δt = 5 µs. Basis-state fidelities Fe and Fl are calculated from signal-to-noise ratio as Fe,l = (S+N)/(S+2N), where S is the signal after subtracting noise and N is the noise. The average computational-basis fidelity is Fpoles = (Fe+Fl)/2. For superposition-state measurements, an unbalanced Mach-Zehnder-interferometer-type pulse sequence is implemented by replacing the π pulse at t6 with two π/2 pulses separated by the same Δt and with relative phase Δβ. The phase Δβ is swept to measure interference for input states with Δα = 0° and Δα = 90°. The visibility V of the interference fringe gives the equatorial-state fidelity Fequator = (1+V)/2. The total conditional fidelity per qubit is FT = (1/3)Fpoles + (2/3)Fequator. The measurement integrates over the optical memory mode through the full prepared ensemble and compares forward and backward retrieval configurations under their respective phase-matching geometries.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: implement a Stark-echo-modulated spin-wave quantum memory in Eu3+:Y2SiO5, using electric-field-induced opposite Stark phases in inversion-related Eu3+ sub-ensembles to suppress unwanted coherent echo emission without removing absorbers, thereby preserving the full optical depth for forward or backward retrieval. The preparation procedure is performed on a 0.1% Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystal with dimensions 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm along the D1, D2, and C2 axes, using Eu3+ ions at site 1. The crystal is cooled to 1.8 K in a cryostat. Optical fields propagate along the C2 axis and are polarized along D1. Copper electrodes attached to the crystal with silver paint provide electric fields parallel to D1. A collinear counter-propagating optical arrangement is aligned with a fiber coupler; optical pulses are generated and modulated with two acousto-optic modulators, and avalanche-photodiode detection is gated with a separate acousto-optic modulator. The ensemble-preparation recipe consists of repeated class cleaning and spin-polarization pulse sequences: 1-ms frequency-chirped optical pulses with 100 µW peak power are applied, with the class-cleaning block repeated 200 times and the spin-polarization blocks repeated 200 times as indicated for the addressed Eu3+ hyperfine transitions. The spatial scope is the optical mode passing through the full 10-mm crystal length along C2, targeting the ensemble absorption feature used as the active memory region rather than isolated microscopic sites. The goal is to determine whether this preparation creates a spectrally isolated absorption feature suitable for the Stark-echo memory protocol, quantified by optical depth and spectral bandwidth from the transmission spectrum.

result_rows.description: The optical depth of the prepared Eu3+ absorption feature used as the active memory transition.
The spectral bandwidth of the prepared Eu3+ absorption feature used for memory operation.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: characterize the Stark control mechanism required for a Stark-echo-modulated spin-wave quantum memory in Eu3+:Y2SiO5, where inversion-related Eu3+ sub-ensembles acquire opposite Stark phases so that a first electric-field pulse can scramble collective emission and a second electric-field pulse can rephase it. The measurement uses the same 0.1% Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystal, 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm along D1, D2, and C2, cooled to 1.8 K, with optical fields propagating along C2 and polarized along D1. Electric fields are applied parallel to D1 using copper electrodes attached with silver paint. The spectrally prepared ensemble from class cleaning and spin polarization is probed over the optical beam path through the full crystal length. Stark modulation is measured with two-pulse photon-echo, four-level photon-echo, and Stark-echo sequences. In the Stark-echo verification, one Stark pulse at time t1 is fixed and the second Stark-pulse area at time t7 is swept; the memory operating point uses a Stark-pulse area of 9.25 V cm^-1 µs. The Stark shift convention is Δν = −L Δµ·E, where Δν is the optical-frequency shift, L is the local-field correction factor, Δµ is the difference in permanent electric dipole moments between the two levels, and E is the applied electric field. For a Stark pulse of duration τS and electric field ES, the two inversion-related sub-ensembles accumulate relative phase 2φS = 2(Δµ·ES/ℏ)τS. The goal is to calibrate the linear Stark coefficient that determines the phase scrambling and rephasing used in the memory sequence.

result_rows.description: The measured optical-frequency Stark shift coefficient for the addressed Eu3+:Y2SiO5 transition under an electric field along D1.
The one-standard-deviation uncertainty of the measured linear Stark coefficient.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: test forward retrieval in the Stark-echo spin-wave quantum memory, in which four optical π pulses and two Stark pulses are used to suppress the ordinary four-level echo and retrieve a Stark echo while preserving the full prepared optical depth of the Eu3+:Y2SiO5 ensemble. The active medium is a 0.1% Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystal, 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm along D1, D2, and C2, cooled to 1.8 K. Eu3+ site-1 hyperfine levels form the four-level scheme. Optical pulses propagate along C2 with polarization along D1. The electric field is applied along D1 through copper electrodes attached with silver paint. The prepared absorption feature has its optical mode extending through the 10-mm crystal length along C2. The forward-retrieval sequence uses an input signal at t0 followed by a first Stark pulse at t1, optical π pulses at t2 and t3 to transfer optical coherence to the ground-state spin coherence |±1/2>g ↔ |±3/2>g, optical π pulses at t5 and t6 to transfer through the excited-state spin coherence |±3/2>e ↔ |±5/2>e, and a second Stark pulse at t7. The Stark pulse area used for memory operation is 9.25 V cm^-1 µs. The forward phase-matching condition is k_echo = k0 − k2 − k3 + k5 + k6, where ki is the wave vector of the optical pulse at time ti; the echo time is t8 = t0 − t2 − t3 + t5 + t6. Direct avalanche-photodiode detection is used for the retrieved Stark-echo intensity, with the detection window gated by an acousto-optic modulator. The timing of the π pulses is adjusted to temporally separate the Stark echo from four-level-echo background; the reported memory-efficiency point is evaluated at a storage/retrieval time of 29 µs. Coherence dynamics are measured by heterodyne detection of Stark-echo decay curves while independently varying the intervals t6−t3 and t5−t2 over the plotted range from about 20 µs to 60 µs. The data are fitted with ηSE = ηretrieval ηpm ηcontrol^4 ηdecay, where ηSE is total memory efficiency, ηretrieval is the optical-depth-dependent retrieval factor, ηpm is phase-matching efficiency, ηcontrol is the population-transfer efficiency of each π pulse, and ηdecay is the decoherence term. For forward retrieval ηretrieval = d^2 exp(−d), with d = αL the optical depth. The decoherence model is ηdecay = exp[−Γ13^2(t5−t2)^2/(2 ln2/π^2)] exp[−Γ35^2(t6−t3)^2/(2 ln2/π^2) − 2γ(t6−t3)], where Γ13 is the inhomogeneous linewidth of |±1/2>g ↔ |±3/2>g, Γ35 is the inhomogeneous linewidth of |±3/2>e ↔ |±5/2>e, and γ is the effective optical decoherence rate. For the co-propagating forward geometry, ηpm is taken as unity when extracting ηcontrol.

The extracted population-transfer efficiency per optical π pulse for the forward geometry, inferred from the forward memory efficiency and decay model with phase matching set to unity.

report_experiments.experiment_description: Central concept: test backward retrieval in the Stark-echo spin-wave quantum memory, using Stark phase scrambling and rephasing to enable a retrieval direction that avoids the reabsorption-limited forward-emission geometry while retaining the full prepared optical depth of the Eu3+:Y2SiO5 ensemble. The active medium is a 0.1% Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystal, 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm along D1, D2, and C2, cooled to 1.8 K. Optical fields address Eu3+ site-1 hyperfine transitions, propagate along the C2 axis in a collinear counter-propagating geometry, and are polarized along D1. Electric fields are applied along D1 using copper electrodes attached with silver paint. The optical mode passes through the 10-mm crystal length and defines the active memory region. The backward-retrieval pulse sequence contains the same Stark-echo elements as the forward protocol: input signal at t0, first Stark pulse at t1, two optical π pulses at t2 and t3, two later optical π pulses at t5 and t6, and a second Stark pulse at t7, with the memory Stark-pulse area set to 9.25 V cm^-1 µs. To target backward phase matching, the propagation direction of the π pulse at t5 is reversed, the two π pulses at t5 and t6 are interchanged relative to the forward sequence, and the timing is adjusted to separate background four-level echoes from the Stark echo by spatial and temporal discrimination. The phase-matching convention is k_echo = k0 − k2 − k3 + k5 + k6, where ki is the optical wave vector at ti; the echo time is t8 = t0 − t2 − t3 + t5 + t6. Direct avalanche-photodiode detection measures the retrieved Stark-echo intensity, and heterodyne detection records Stark-echo decay profiles while varying t6−t3 and t5−t2 over the plotted range from about 25 µs to 60 µs. The reported memory-efficiency point is evaluated at 23 µs. Decay data are fitted with ηSE = ηretrieval ηpm ηcontrol^4 ηdecay, with backward retrieval factor ηretrieval = [1 − exp(−d)]^2, d = αL, and ηdecay = exp[−Γ13^2(t5−t2)^2/(2 ln2/π^2)] exp[−Γ35^2(t6−t3)^2/(2 ln2/π^2) − 2γ(t6−t3)], where Γ13 and Γ35 are the ground- and excited-state spin-transition inhomogeneous linewidths and γ is the effective optical decoherence rate.

result_rows.description: The directly measured backward Stark-echo memory efficiency at the specified storage/retrieval time.
The one-standard-deviation uncertainty of the directly measured backward Stark-echo memory efficiency.
The fitted inhomogeneous linewidth of the |±3/2>e ↔ |±5/2>e spin transition from backward Stark-echo decay measurements.
The one-standard-deviation uncertainty of the fitted Γ35 linewidth from backward Stark-echo decay measurements.
The fitted inhomogeneous linewidth of the |±1/2>g ↔ |±3/2>g spin transition from backward Stark-echo decay measurements.
The one-standard-deviation uncertainty of the fitted Γ13 linewidth from backward Stark-echo decay measurements.
The extracted combined factor ηpm ηcontrol^4 for the backward geometry, where ηpm is phase-matching efficiency and ηcontrol is the population-transfer efficiency per π pulse.

per_file.paper_title: Observation of end-to-end pumping in a quasiperiodic Fibonacci-type photonic chain

expected_output.experiment_description: Fabricate the photonic platform for a minimal-control quasiperiodic Fibonacci-type end-to-end pump: an array of N = 11 evanescently coupled optical waveguides in transparent glass, where nearest-neighbor separations implement a Fibonacci-type Sturmian sequence with two target center-to-center spacings dA = 10 µm and dB = 7 µm. The sequence is defined by χ_i = sgn[cos(2π i τ^{-1} + π τ^{-1} + φ) − cos(π τ^{-1})], where τ = (1 + sqrt(5))/2 is the golden ratio, φ is the phason angle, positive χ_i assigns spacing dB, negative χ_i assigns spacing dA, and i labels neighboring waveguide bonds. The central device idea is that two selected phason configurations support a localized defect-like pumping state at opposite ends, so the platform should realize uniform single-mode guides whose separations can encode the quasiperiodic hopping pattern and allow only waveguides 2 and 10 to be bent for pumping. Use femtosecond-laser direct writing with a Menlo Systems BlueCut fs laser at 1030 nm central wavelength, approximately 350 fs pulse duration, and 1 MHz repetition rate. Focus the writing beam into the bulk glass with a 40× objective of NA = 0.6. Mount the substrate on a high-precision three-axis translation stage and translate it along the propagation direction z at 40 mm/s while keeping the laser focus fixed. Write all guides at approximately 100 µm depth below the glass surface. Set the writing laser power to the paper's optimized value for single-mode guiding at the 780 nm probe wavelength; the numerical writing power is not reported. Fabricate two nominally identical samples for each reported lattice configuration, including defect-free, bent, straight, and structurally defected arrays, so the spatial scope is the full 11-waveguide chain in each sample and reproducibility is assessed by independent fabrication and optical measurement of paired samples.

single_mode_guiding_at_780_nm.description: Whether the direct-written waveguides support single-mode guiding at the probe wavelength.

mode_field_diameter_1_over_e2_um.description: The measured Gaussian mode-field diameter of the fabricated waveguides using the 1/e^2 intensity convention.

refractive_index_modification.description: The estimated refractive-index change induced in the glass by the direct-writing process.

propagation_loss_db_per_cm.description: The estimated optical propagation loss of the fabricated waveguides.

paired_sample_reproducibility_verified.description: Whether nominally identical paired samples for the reported configurations were independently fabricated and measured under the same optical conditions.

expected_output.experiment_description: Calibrate the evanescent coupling law used to map the quasiperiodic Fibonacci-type photonic chain onto a tight-binding Hamiltonian for the minimal end-to-end pump. Fabricate isolated two-waveguide directional couplers in the same transparent glass substrate and with the same femtosecond direct-writing conditions as the full N = 11 lattices: 1030 nm, approximately 350 fs, 1 MHz writing laser; 40× NA = 0.6 focusing objective; 40 mm/s sample translation; approximately 100 µm writing depth; and the same optimized writing power used for the pump arrays. Prepare couplers with different center-to-center separations d_ij spanning the range shown in the calibration plot, approximately 9–16 µm. Inject 780 nm light into one waveguide of each two-guide coupler and measure the two output intensities at the end facet. Extract the coupling strength J_ij in mm^{-1} from the power oscillation according to coupled-mode theory.
